(Section)

When the servant is saved from the trial of doubts and desires, he attains the two greatest objectives sought, through which his happiness, success and perfection are realized. They are guidance (al-huda) and mercy (al-rahma).

Allah the Exalted said about Musa and his servant:

﴿So they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Us.﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

So He combined for him mercy and knowledge. This is parallel to the saying of the People of the Cave: ﴿Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair.﴾ [al-Kahf: 10].

Indeed, rushd (right direction) is knowledge of what benefits, and acting upon it. Guidance and rushd, when each is mentioned alone, includes the other, and when the two are mentioned together, each is distinguished. Guidance is knowledge of the truth, and rushd is acting upon it. Their opposites are ghayy (error) and following desire.

Rushd is also contrasted with harm and evil. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or right direction."﴾ [al-Jinn: 21].

And the believers among the jinn said: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them right direction.﴾ [al-Jinn: 10].

So rushd is opposed to ghayy, as in His saying: ﴿And if they see the way of right direction, they will not adopt it as a way; but if they see the way of error, they will adopt it as a way.﴾ [al-A'raf: 146].

And it is opposed to harm and evil, as mentioned earlier, because ghayy is the cause of evil and harm befalling its possessor.

Thus harm and evil are the outcome and fruit of transgression, just as mercy and success are the outcome and fruit of guidance.

For this reason each of them is contrasted with its opposite and the cause of its opposite: guidance is contrasted with misguidance, as in His saying: ﴿He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.﴾ [al-Nahl: 93], and His saying: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide one who misleads.﴾ [al-Nahl: 37]. And this is frequent.

It is also contrasted with misguidance and punishment, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor suffer.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123].

So He contrasted guidance with misguidance and wretchedness.

Glory be to Him, He combined guidance with success, and guidance with mercy, just as He combines misguidance with wretchedness and misguidance with punishment, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness.﴾ [al-Qamar: 47].

So dalal (misguidance) is the opposite of guidance, and su'ur (the blaze/punishment) is the punishment, which is the opposite of mercy.

And He said: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance — indeed, for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124].

The point is: whoever is saved from the trial of doubts and desires, guidance and mercy, and guidance and success, are combined for him.

Allah the Exalted said about His friends: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 8]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Musa, he took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.﴾ [al-A'raf: 154]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe with certainty.﴾ [al-A'raf: 203]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There was in their stories a lesson for those of understanding. It was not a narration invented, but a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ [Yunus: 57].

So His saying "This is insights from your Lord" is general and unrestricted, while His saying "and guidance and mercy for a people who believe with certainty" is specific to the people of certainty.

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ [Yunus: 57].

Its parallel in specificity is His saying: ﴿Guidance for the righteous.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], and His saying: ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16].

Also similar is His saying: ﴿This is an explanation for mankind, and guidance and instruction for the righteous.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 138].

He has informed that guidance is general for all accountable people. He said: ﴿They follow only assumption and what their souls desire, while there has already come to them from their Lord guidance.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

[Section: The Station of Wajd (Ecstatic Feeling)]

Among the stations of "You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help" is the station of wajd (ecstatic feeling).

It is established in the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has three qualities will find the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger become dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for the sake of Allah; and that he hates to return to disbelief after Allah has saved him from it, just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire."

The author of the Manazil cited the words of Allah concerning the People of the Cave: ﴿And We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke besides Him any deity. We would have certainly spoken, then, an excessive transgression."﴾ [al-Kahf: 14]

This is one of the best forms of inference and citation. These people were among their disbelieving people, in the service of their disbelieving king. Then, as soon as they found the reality of faith and divine success and tasted its sweetness, and it penetrated their hearts, they stood up from among their people and said: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Kahf: 14], and so on.

The "strengthening of their hearts" (al-rabt 'ala qulubihim) includes binding them firmly with patience and steadfastness, and strengthening and supporting them with the light of faith, until they endured abandoning the homes of their people and leaving the ease of life they had been in. They fled with their religion to the cave.

The strengthening of the heart is the opposite of abandonment (al-khidhlan). Abandonment is when the bond of divine success is loosened from the person, so he becomes heedless of the remembrance of his Lord, follows his desire, and his affair becomes lost (furuṭ).

The strengthening of the heart is binding it with the bond of divine success, so it stays connected to the remembrance of its Lord, follows His pleasure, and its scattered concerns are gathered. For this reason the author cited this verse in the station of wajd.

The Shaykh made the station of wajd distinct from the station of wujud, as will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. According to the people (of Sufism), wujud is attaining the reality of a thing, while wajd is what meets the heart and comes upon it from the visitations of love, longing, reverence and glorification, and what follows from these.

The mawajid (intense experiences) are, in their view, above wajd, since wajd is a chance encounter, whereas the mawajid are the fruits of the litanies (awrad). Whenever the litanies increase, the mawajid grow stronger.

Wujud, in their view, is above all of that. It is attaining the reality of the sought object, and it does not occur except after the extinction of human nature and the complete stripping away of the soul's rulings.

Al-Junayd said: "The knowledge of tawhid is separate from its existence, and its existence is separate from its knowledge."

By "separation" he does not mean contradiction or opposition, for it corresponds to it in the way knowledge corresponds to the known.

Rather, by separation he means that the state of the monotheist, his taste of tawhid, and his heart being dyed with its state, is something beyond his knowledge of it and his awareness of it. The separation between them is like the separation between the knowledge of longing, trust (tawakkul), fear and the like, and their realities and their ecstatic experiences.

The levels are four. The weakest of them is tawajud, which is a kind of artificiality, contrivance and forced summoning.

They differed about it: is it accepted from its practitioner or not? There are two opinions.

One group said: it is not accepted from its practitioner, and he is rebuked for it, because of the artificiality and affectation it contains, which contradicts the path of the truthful. The foundation of this matter is pure sincerity.

Another group said: it is accepted from its practitioner if his intention is to summon the reality, not to imitate its people. They argued with the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr weeping over the captives of Badr and the ransom they accepted from them: "Tell me, what makes you weep? If I find weeping, I will weep; and if not, I will feign weeping." They also transmitted a report: "Weep; and if you cannot weep, then feign weeping."

They said: artificiality and contrivance are unavoidable at the beginning of the journey and the path, since the one at the beginning is not required what is required of the one who has attained the state. Whoever considers it with the intention of attaining the reality for one who watches for wajd is not blamed. Tawajud occurs through the outward movements the servant forces upon himself, and "the mawajid" are the inward rulings for one who interprets them.

The second level: the mawajid, which are the results and fruits of the litanies.

The third level: wajd, which is the fruit of the deeds of the hearts, such as love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah, just as the Prophet ﷺ made it the fruit of Allah and His Messenger becoming dearer to the servant than anything else, and the fruit of loving a person for His sake, and of hating to return to disbelief just as one hates to be thrown into the Fire. This wajd is the fruit of these heart deeds, which are love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah.

The fourth level: wujud, which is the highest peak of the station of ihsan. One ascends to it from the station of ihsan. When the witnessing of his Worshipped One overcomes his heart, to the point that he almost sees Him, and this becomes firmly established, it becomes for him a disposition that extinguishes the rulings of his soul, replaces them with other rulings and a second nature, until it is as if he has been created in a new genesis other than his first, and born with a new birth.

It is reported from the Messiah, peace be upon him, that he said: "O Children of Israel, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven until you are born twice."

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, mention this, and he explained it by saying that birth is of two kinds. One is this well-known birth, and the second is the birth of the heart and the spirit, and their emerging from the placenta of the soul and the darkness of nature.

He said: Since this birth came through the Messenger, he is like a father to the believers. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "The Prophet is nearer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them."

He said: The meaning of this verse and this reading is in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], since the motherhood of his wives toward them is a branch of his fatherhood.

He said: So the shaykh, the teacher and the educator is the father of the spirit, and the parent is the father of the body.

It is said of love: wajd; of anger: mawjidah; and of attainment: wijdan and wujud.

(Benefit: the origin of the word dhāt)

The origin of this word is the feminine of dhū, meaning "possessor" (ṣāḥib). So dhāt, in its original sense, means "the possessor of such-and-such." For this reason, one does not say dhāt al-shay' (the dhāt of a thing) except for what has attributes and qualities attached to it, as if one were saying "the possessor of these attributes and qualities."

For this reason, a group of grammarians, among them Ibn Burhān and others, objected to the usage of the Uṣūlīs (jurists of legal theory) in saying al-dhāt (the dhāt), and they said that the definite article has no place here, just as one does not say al-dhū in place of dhū.

This objection is correct. The excuse for them is that the term dhāt, in their technical usage, came to denote the thing itself, its reality, and its essence. When they used it in the sense of "self" and "reality," they made it definite with the article and stripped it of its original sense. It is from here that al-Suhaylī charged them with error.

This usage and stripping of meaning is a technical matter, not a linguistic one, for the Arabs hardly say "I saw the thing itself (li-ʿaynihi)" or "its self (nafsihi)." Rather, they say that only of what is attributed to it and comes from its side.

This is like the phrase "janb" (side) of a thing: when they say "fī janb Allāh" (in the side of God), they mean only what is attributed to Him, namely His path, His pleasure, and His obedience, and they mean nothing else at all.

So when the theologians agreed to use dhāt to mean the self and the reality, whoever thought that this is what is meant by his saying

"Three lies in the dhāt of God"

and his saying "and that was in the dhāt of the God (al-Ilāh)"

erred, and deserved to be corrected. Rather, dhāt here is like janb in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Oh, my grief, that I neglected in the side of God﴾.

Do you not see that it is not fitting to say here "I neglected in the self of God and His reality," whereas it is fitting to say "he neglected in the dhāt of God," just as one says "he did such-and-such in the dhāt of God," "he was killed in the dhāt of God Most High," and "he was patient in the dhāt of God"?

Reflect on this, for it is one of the rare and strange investigations for which fingers are praised. And God is the Granter of success and the Helper.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 18, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog," and they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog."﴾

It has been said that the purpose of the waw (conjunction "and") here is to indicate the eight. This may bear two meanings. The first: this [is the purpose]. The second: that the entry of the waw here serves as a sign that their speech is complete at their saying "seven," and then he begins with His saying "and the eighth of them was their dog," which entails confirming their saying "seven," as when someone says to you, "Zayd is a jurist," and you reply, "and a grammarian." This is the view chosen by al-Suhayli, and the discussion of it has already passed. This [second meaning] only holds if His saying "and the eighth of them was their dog" is not included in what is reported as said, and the apparent meaning is the opposite, and God knows best.

(Section)

As for the nineteenth question, which is the entry of the waw in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the People of the Book greet you with salam, say: 'And upon you'" (wa 'alaykum).

Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Many people have raised an objection to it, as mentioned in the question, and they said the correct wording is to omit the waw and say "alaykum."

Al-Khattabi said: The majority of the narrators of hadith transmit it with the waw, while Ibn 'Uyaynah transmits it without it, and that is the correct form. This is because when the waw is omitted, their very saying is returned to them unchanged, whereas with the waw there is a sharing and an inclusion in what they said, since the waw is a conjunctive particle and the joining of two things.

I say: The meaning of what al-Khattabi indicated is that the waw in such a context requires the affirmation of the first clause and the addition of the second to it, as when you say, "Zayd is a writer," and the addressee says, "and a poet," which entails affirming writing for him plus the addition of the description of poetry. Likewise, if you say to a man, "So-and-so is fond of you," and he replies, "and benevolent toward me," the number of the People of the Cave [is seven].

From here al-Suhayli deduced in al-Rawd: "The number of the People of the Cave is seven, for God, exalted is He, joined the dog to them with the particle waw," saying: ﴿and the eighth of them was their dog﴾, and did not mention a waw in the preceding part of their speech, and the waw requires the affirmation of the first clause. What he deduced is good, except that it is only valid if the clause introduced by the waw is not part of their saying, but rather He, glorified is He, has reported that they said "seven," and then informed that the eighth of them was the dog; in that case it is an affirmation of what they said and an announcement that the dog was the eighth. But if the statement about the dog is part of their saying, and they said "this and this," then what he said does not appear, and the waw in that case implies neither affirmation nor confirmation, so consider it.

As for his saying that the hadith scholars transmit it with the waw: this hadith was narrated by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the Jews greet you with salam, one of them only says, 'al-sam 'alaykum' (death upon you), so say, 'and upon you.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, and Abu Dawud. Abu Dawud said: "Likewise Malik narrated it from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, and al-Thawri narrated it from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar and said in it, 'wa 'alaykum.'" End of his words. It was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i in the same way, and Muslim narrated it.

In some of its chains, it says, "Say: 'alayka" without the waw. The hadith of Malik that Abu Dawud mentioned is recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, and the hadith of Sufyan al-Thawri is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim); all of them have the waw.

As for what al-Khattabi indicated from the hadith of Ibn 'Uyaynah, it was narrated by al-Nasa'i in his Sunan without the waw.

Once this is understood, the entry of the waw in the hadith entails no objectionable implication at all. This is because the greeting with which they greet the Muslims ultimately conveys the announcement that death has befallen them and a request for it, since al-sam means death. So when they greet the Muslim with it and he returns it to them, it is a matter of retaliation and justice, and the import of his reply is: "We do not die before you; rather, you too will die. What you wished for us has befallen you." Better than this is to say: the entry of the waw is not an affirmation of the content of their greeting; rather, it is a return of it and an affirmation of it to them, i.e., "and we too invoke upon you what you invoked upon us." Their invocation has already taken effect, so when the responder returns it to them with his saying "and upon you," there is in the entry of the waw a subtle secret, which is the indication that what you wished for us and invoked upon us is itself returned to you, not any other greeting. So the entry of the waw conveys this great benefit. Consider this against the case of invoking good: when someone says "God forgive you," and the other replies "and you," the meaning is that this same supplication is from me to you. If you said "God forgive you" and he said "you" (without "and"), there would be no indication that the second supplication is the very first one. Reflect upon this, for it is very subtle.

On this basis, the correct form is to retain the waw, as it is established in the Sahih and the Sunan. This is what has become clear to me regarding this wording. Whoever finds something should add it in the margin, and God will thank him and his servants will appreciate his effort, for the aim is to reach the correct view; once it is manifest, whatever contradicts it is placed beneath the feet. We have treated this question fully, to the extent possible for us, in the book Tahdhib al-Sunan.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 18, verses 23–24:

Allah has rebuked His Messenger ﷺ when he said to those among the People of the Book who asked him about things, "Tomorrow I will inform you," without saying "if Allah wills." Revelation was therefore withheld from him for a month, and then this was revealed to him: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [with the condition], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

That is: if you forget that exception after your statement, then mention it when you remember. This is the meaning of the verse, and it is what Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) intended by the validity of the delayed exception (al-istithnaʾ al-mutarakhkhi, the exception made later). Neither Ibn ʿAbbas nor anyone below him ever said that if a man says to his wife, "You are divorced," or to his slave, "You are free," and then after a year says, "If Allah wills," that she is not divorced and the slave is not freed. Whoever transmitted that from Ibn ʿAbbas, or from any scholar at all, was entirely mistaken, and did not understand Ibn ʿAbbas's meaning. The point is that the exception is not restricted to oaths, neither in the Shariʿah, nor in custom, nor in linguistic usage.

(Section)

The interpretation of the verse according to the majority of the exegetes is: you should not say of anything, "I will do such-and-such," until you say, "If Allah wills." So if you forget to say it, then say it whenever you remember it. This is the delayed exception which Ibn ʿAbbas permitted and on which he interpreted the verse. And it is the correct view.

Whoever did not understand his words erred about him, and it was transmitted from him that if a man says to his wife, "You are divorced three times," or says, "All four of my wives are divorced," then after a year says, "except one," or, "except Zaynab," this exception benefits him. But Allah has protected from this even those far below the young students of Ibn ʿAbbas, let alone the sea of learning, the scholar of the Ummah, whom Allah gave understanding of the religion and taught interpretation. How often do people transmit false doctrines from scholars through their deficient understandings!

Were we to mention all of that, it would be very long; and if Allah grants help, we would devote a book to it.

What the exegetes agreed upon is: the People of Makkah asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Spirit, the People of the Cave, and Dhu al-Qarnayn. He said, "I will inform you tomorrow," and did not say, "If Allah wills." So revelation was delayed for some days, and then this verse was revealed.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others said: its meaning is: if you forget the exception and then remember, make the exception.

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The exception is permitted up to a year.

ʿIkrimah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: ﴿And remember your Lord when you become angry﴾. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: this refers to the prayer; that is, if you forget the prayer, then pray it whenever you remember it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 18, verse 28:

Patience (al-sabr) in linguistic usage means restraint and withholding. From this comes the expression "so-and-so was killed sabran," meaning he was held back and restrained. From it also is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And keep yourself patient along with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]; that is, restrain yourself along with them.

Patience, then, is restraining the soul from distress and discontent; restraining the tongue from complaint; and restraining the limbs from disorder.

It is of three kinds: patience in obedience to Allah; patience in refraining from disobedience to Allah; and patience in the trial of Allah. The first two are patience concerning what falls within a person's acquisition (kasb). The third is patience concerning what is not within the servant's acquisition.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: The patience of Yusuf in resisting the advances of the wife of al-Aziz was more perfect than his patience over his brothers casting him into the well, selling him, and separating him from his father. For these were matters that befell him without his choice, in which he had no acquisition, and in which the servant has no recourse other than patience.

As for his patience in refraining from sin, it is patience of choice, contentment, and fighting against the soul, especially with the circumstances that strengthen the motives toward compliance. He was young, and the motive of youth toward it is strong; he was unmarried, with nothing to compensate for him and restrain his desire; he was a stranger, and a stranger does not feel shame in the land of his estrangement what one among his companions, acquaintances and family would feel shame of; he was a slave, and a slave's restraint is not like a free man's restraint; the woman was beautiful and of high rank; she was his mistress; the watchful guardian was absent; and she was the one inviting him to herself.

She was eager for this with the utmost eagerness, and yet she threatened him with prison and humiliation if he did not comply. Despite all these motives, he was patient by choice, and out of preference for what is with Allah. And where is this from his patience in the well over what was not of his acquisition?

He used to say: patience in performing acts of obedience is more perfect than patience in avoiding what is forbidden, and it is superior; for the benefit of performing an act of obedience is more beloved to the Lawgiver than the benefit of abandoning disobedience. And the harm of not obeying is more hateful and more detestable to Him than the harm of the existence of disobedience.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, has a work on this in which he established it in about twenty aspects. It is not the place to mention them.

(Section: on the linguistic meaning of patience, the derivation of this word and its conjugation)

The root of this word is prevention and restraint. Thus patience is restraining the soul from distress, the tongue from complaint, and the limbs from slapping the cheeks, tearing garments and the like. It is said: sabara yasbiru sabran, and sabara nafsahu. The Exalted said: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf].

And ʿAntarah said:

"So I was patient, knowing of that, free-born, / She stands firm when the soul of the coward rises (in fear)."

He means: I restrained a knowing soul, and it is the soul of a free man who disdains, not the soul of a slave who has no disdain. His saying "tarsu" means: she remains firm and calm when the soul of the coward is alarmed and agitated. It is said: "sabartu fulanan" when I held him back, and "sabbartuhu" (with the doubled letter) when I compelled him to patience. In the hadith of the one who held a man while another killed him: "the killer is killed and the one who holds is held" (yuqtal al-qatil wa yusbar al-sabir), meaning he is confined for death just as the one who held him was confined for death. "Sabartu al-rajul" means I killed him by sabr, that is, I held him for killing; and "sabartuhu" and "asbartuhu" mean I confined him for oath-taking. From this is the sound hadith: "Whoever swears an oath of sabr to seize by it the property of a Muslim man will meet Allah while He is angry with him." From this also is the hadith about the qasamah: "and his oath is not made to be sabr where the oaths are made to be sabr." Al-musbarah is the oath sworn upon; and in the hadith he forbade al-musbarah, which is a sheep, a chicken and the like that are restrained for death, tied and shot until they die.

The verb of this category is sabira yasbiru, with fatha in the past and kasra in the present. As for sabira yasburu with damma in the present, it means guaranteeing; al-sabir is the guarantor, as if he confined himself to bear the loss. From it the saying "asbarani," meaning "he made me a guarantor."

It is said the root means strength and hardness. From it is the sabr (aloe) known as a medicine because of its extreme bitterness and repulsiveness.

Al-Asmaʿi said: "When a man meets hardship in its entirety, it is said: he met it with its sabr."

From it is al-sabr (with a damma on the sad) for land that is rocky, because of its hardness and firmness; from it the lava-field is called Umm Sabar; and from it the saying: "The people fell into a sabur matter," with doubled ba, meaning a hard matter; and from it "sabarat al-shita'" (with the ba lightened and the ra doubled) for the intensity of its cold.

It is said it derives from gathering and compressing: the patient person gathers himself and compresses himself against panic and distress. From it are "sabrat al-ta'am" (a heap of food) and "sabarat al-hijarah" (a heap of stones).

The verification is that patience contains the three meanings: restraint, hardness and compression. It is said "sabara" when one brings patience; "tasabbara" when one forces and seeks it; "istabara" when one acquires and practises it; "sabara" (in the form of mufa'alah) when one stands against his opponent in a position of patience; and "sabbara nafsahu wa ghayrahu" with doubling when one compels the self or another to patience. The active participles are sabir, sabbar, sabur, musabir, and mustabir: musabir from sabara (form III), mustabir from istabara, sabir from sabara; and sabbar and sabur are intensive patterns of the triliteral, like darrab and daruub. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

Whoever reflects on the state of this creation will find them all, except a very small minority, whose hearts have been made heedless of the remembrance of Allah, who followed their desires, and whose affairs and interests became ﴿fruṭan﴾, that is, they neglected what benefits them and brings about their righteousness, and occupied themselves with what does not benefit them but rather brings them harm, both swiftly and later.

Allah the Glorified commanded His Messenger not to obey these people. The obedience to the Messenger is not complete except by not obeying them, for they only call to what resembles them: following desire, heedlessness of the remembrance of Allah, and heedlessness of the Hereafter. Whenever following desire is joined to the Hereafter, it produces every evil between them; and it is often the case that one of them is joined with the other and does not part from it.

Whoever reflects on the corruption of the states of the world, generally and specifically, will find it arising from these two roots: heedlessness comes between the servant and the perception and knowledge of the truth, so he becomes one of the misguided; and following desire prevents him from intending and pursuing the truth, so he becomes one of those upon whom is wrath.

As for those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, they are those to whom Allah granted knowledge of the truth and submission to it, and preference for it over all else in action. These are the people of the path of salvation, and whoever else is on the path of destruction. For this reason Allah commanded us to say every day and night, many times: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾.

(Section)

In the verse there is clear refutation of the two groups and nullification of their doctrines: for He, the Glorified, made the servant's heart heedless of His remembrance, and so he became heedless.

Causing heedlessness is the act of Allah, and heedlessness is the act of the servant; then He informed of his following his desire, and that is truly the act of the servant.

The Qadariyyah distort this text and its like by naming and knowing: they say the meaning of ﴿We made his heart heedless﴾ is "we named him heedless," or "we found him heedless," that is, "we knew him to be so."

This is from their distortion; rather, aghfalnahu is like aqamtahu, aqadtahu, aghnaytahu and afqartahu, meaning we made him so.

As for af'altuhu or awjadtuhu (I found him so) like ahmadtuhu, ajnabtuhu, abkhaltuhu and a'jiztuhu, these never occur in the acts of Allah; they occur only in the acts of one who is incapable, who finds someone a coward, miserly or incapable, so that its meaning is "I found him so."

Does it occur to the heart of one who supplicates, "O Allah, empower me, or inspire me, or grant me, or teach me," that this means naming him or knowing him so? Is this not lying against him and against the One he calls? Reasonable people know by necessary knowledge that the supplicant asks Allah to create that for him, to will it for him and to empower him to it. Even the Qadari, when his innovation departs from him and what he took on from his shaykhs and predecessors, and his natural disposition remains, does not think of anything other than this.

Furthermore, it is impossible that the servant should be the one who makes himself heedless of something, for his making himself heedless of it is conditioned on his awareness of it, and that contradicts his being heedless of it. Unlike Allah causing him to be heedless, which does not contradict His knowledge of what the servant is heedless of; and unlike the servant's heedlessness, which occurs only with his lack of awareness of what he is heedless of. This is quite evident. Thus it is established that causing heedlessness is the act of Allah toward His servant, and heedlessness is the act of the servant.

(Benefit)

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾.

This verse combines the entrusting of all affairs, their benefit and harm, their good and evil, to the God, His power be exalted, with affirmation of the realities of obligation and the establishment of the principles of the Law in a rational way.

Are you not, in this, more rightly guided in path and more upright in speech than one who makes nature a prevention and the seal a repulsion, and then denies obligations by his claim? The people have divided into groups on this station. Some went that the forsaken are prevented and repelled, having no power to respond to those who call to the truth, and yet they are nonetheless obligated. This is a grave matter and a great affair, and it is a slander against the laws and a nullification of the calls. The Exalted said: ﴿And what prevented people from believing when the guidance came to them?﴾

And Iblis said: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ We seek refuge in Allah from bad thinking about the places of danger. Other groups of misguided people went that the servant disobeys while the Lord is averse to what he does. This is confusion in the divine rulings and a rivalry against lordship. Had the Lord not willed from the wicked what He knew of them in His eternity, He would not have created them while knowing them. How so, when He has perfected their strengths, supplied them with provisions and weapons, and facilitated for them the path of deviation from rectitude?

If it is said: did He do this to them so that they would obey Him?

We say: how can that be correct when He knew that they would disobey Him, destroy themselves, destroy His friends and prophets, and be wretched with a wretchedness in which they will never be happy? And if a master knew, from revelation or from the report of a prophet, that if he provided his slave with wealth he would become insolent, flee and commit highway robbery, yet he provided him with wealth claiming that he wants from him the building of bridges and mosques, and he himself says: I know with certainty that he will not do that—this master is corrupting his slave, not benefiting him, by the agreement of people of understanding. Thus the two factions have strayed and the two groups have gone astray: one objected to the legal principles, and the other rivaled the rulings of lordship. The moderate and the successful said: what Allah wills from His servants is what He knows they will come to, but He did not strip them of their capacity nor prevent them from their rightful paths. Thus the Law remained in its place, and belief flowed in the divine rulings in their correct form.

(Section)

Nothing is more effective in saving one from the punishment of Allah the Mighty and Majestic than the remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. They said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah?" He said: "Not even if he strikes with his sword until it breaks."

There is no doubt that the heart rusts as copper and silver and others rust, and its polish is by remembrance: it polishes it until it leaves it like a white mirror.

When it is abandoned, it rusts; when it is polished, it shines.

The heart rusts from two things, heedlessness and sin, and is polished by two things, seeking forgiveness and remembrance.

Whoever's heedlessness dominates most of his time, the rust accumulates upon his heart, and its rust is according to his heedlessness. When the heart rusts, the forms of knowledge are not impressed upon it as they are; so it sees falsehood in the form of truth and truth in the form of falsehood, because when rust has accumulated upon it, it is darkened, and the forms of realities do not appear in it as they are.

When rust accumulates on it and blackens, and the veil (ran) covers it, its perception and understanding are corrupted: it accepts no truth and denies no falsehood.

This is the greatest punishment of the heart.

The root of this lies in heedlessness and following desire, for they extinguish the light of the heart and blind its sight. The Exalted said: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who followed his desire, and whose affair was fruṭan﴾.

When the servant wishes to follow a man, let him look: is he of the people of remembrance or of the heedless? Is his ruler desire or revelation?

If his ruler is desire and he is of the heedless, then his affair is fruṭ.

The meaning of fruṭ has been explained as neglect, that is, his affair which must be upheld and attended to, and in which lies his right guidance and success, is lost and neglected. It has been explained as excess, that is, he has exceeded in destruction. It has been explained as opposition to the truth.

All these sayings are close in meaning.

The intended meaning: Allah the Glorified and Exalted forbade obeying whoever combines these attributes. A man should look at his shaykh, his exemplar and the one he follows. If he finds him so, let him keep away from him; but if he finds him one in whom the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and following the Sunnah predominate, and whose affair is not neglected but who is resolute in his affair, let him hold firmly to his stirrup.

There is no difference between the living and the dead except by remembrance: the likeness of one who remembers his Lord and one who does not is like the living and the dead.

In the Musnad, it is related as a marfu' report: "Increase the remembrance of Allah the Exalted until they say, 'He is mad.'"

Abu al-ʿAbbas Thaʿlab was asked about the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We made his heart heedless of Our remembrance﴾, and he said: "We made it heedless."

He said: "In speech it may be said: aghfaltuhu, meaning I named him heedless, and I found him heedless."

I say: al-ghafl is an empty thing; al-ard al-ghafl is land with no marks; al-kitab al-ghafl is a book with no vowel-marks on it.

So aghfalnahu means: We left him heedless of the remembrance, empty of it. This is leaving him in his original state of non-existence, because the Glorified did not will for him the remembrance, so he remained heedless; heedlessness is his attribute.

The causing of heedlessness is Allah's act in him by His will, and the absence of His will for his remembrance. Each of them necessitates his heedlessness. When He does not will for him to remember, he does not remember; and when He wills his heedlessness, remembrance is withheld from him.

If it is asked: are heedlessness, disbelief, aversion and the like attributed to the absence of the Lord's will for their opposites, or to the absence of His will for their occurrence?

It is said: the Qur'an has spoken of both. The Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not will to purify﴾.

And He said: ﴿And whoever Allah wills to test, you will not be able to do anything for him against Allah﴾.

And He said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾.

If it is asked: how can the absence of the necessitating cause be the effective cause of the result?

It is said: if the effect is existential, it needs an existential cause; but absence is sufficient with the absence of its cause and its necessitator, so it remains in its original absence. When it is attributed to it, it is in the category of attributing a thing to its evidence: the absence of a cause is evidence of the absence of its effect.

When it is called a necessitator and a cause on this basis, there is no dispute over that; but as for absence being an effect and an agent, that is not so.

This causing of heedlessness resulted in his following his desire and his neglect of his affair.

Mujahid said: "And his affair was fruṭ": that is, loss.

Qatadah said: "He was lost with the greatest loss."

Al-Suddi said: "Destruction."

Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham said: "Amr fruṭ: one who is treated with contempt and neglected. Tafrit is putting forward incapacity."

And again: "Amr fruṭ: one who is treated with contempt and neglected. Tafrit is putting forward incapacity."

Abu Ishaq said: "Whoever puts forward incapacity in a matter has lost it and destroyed it."

Al-Layth said: "Al-fruṭ is the matter one neglects. It is said: every matter of so-and-so is fruṭ."

Al-Farra' said: "Fruṭan means left abandoned: he neglected what should not be neglected, followed what should not be followed, and was heedless of what one should not be heedless of."

(Benefit)

Al-Hasan said: "You will not meet a believer except that he calls himself to account: what did you intend to do? What did you intend to eat? What did you intend to drink?

And the wicked goes forward step by step without calling himself to account."

Qatadah, on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And his affair was fruṭan﴾, said: "He lost himself and was defrauded; yet you see him guarding his wealth while squandering his religion."

(Linguistic benefit)

The Kufans and the Basrans differed concerning (kilā) and (kiltā).

The Basrans held that they are singular nouns indicating the dual, so that a pronoun may refer back to them according to their form, which is the more common usage, and may also refer back according to their meaning, which is less common. Their alif is a radical of the verb and not the alif of the dual, according to them. They have proofs for this, among them that in the three grammatical cases, when they are followed by a noun, they keep one form, whereas the dual does not behave this way. As for their alif turning into a yā' when attached to a pronoun, this does not show that it is the alif of the dual, just as the alif of ʿalā, ilā and ladā is not. This is the view of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh. They also argued with the saying "kilāhumā dhāhib" (both of them is going) rather than "dhāhibān," the form of the dual predicate.

Sībawayh did not rely on this argument, because, as has preceded, when you add the word kull (all), you use a singular predicate even though it indicates the plural, taking the meaning into account, since your saying "kullukum rā'in" (every one of you is a shepherd) is equivalent to "kullu wāḥidin minkum rā'in" (each one of you is a shepherd). So likewise your saying "kilākumā qā'im" means "kullu wāḥidin minkumā qā'im" (each one of you two is standing).

If it is said: "Rather, the predicate was made singular after kull and kilā because they are singular nouns," it is answered: this is refuted by the use of kull and kilā as emphatic words for the plural and the dual. Just as the plural and the dual are not qualified by the singular, so they are not emphasized by it, a fortiori, because emphasis is the repetition of the emphasized thing itself, whereas a qualifier is the thing itself in some respect. What is relied upon by those who support Sībawayh's view is the first argument, despite what is in it, and despite its being opposed by the emphasis of the dual by kilā, and the dual is not emphasized by the singular, as we have established.

If it is said: "The answer to this is that kilā is a noun for the dual, so emphasis by it is appropriate, and agreement is achieved according to its referent, which is the purpose of the speech, so the singularity of the word does no harm?"

It is answered: this is possible for the plural, that its word be singular while its meaning is plural, such as kull and collective nouns like rahṭ and qawm, because the plurals have differed in their forms very greatly: masculine and feminine sound plurals, broken plurals in their various kinds, and what has a singular form as previously explained. So it is no wonder that the form of the word be singular and its meaning plural. As for the dual, it has never differed; rather, it has always kept one pattern wherever it occurs. Therefore it is very far-fetched, indeed impossible, that a singular noun among them should mean a dual. You have nothing but analogy with the plural, and the difference between them has become clear. Thus it is determined that kilā is a dual word whose alif turns into a yā' with a pronoun but not with a noun, because when you attach it to a noun you are excused from turning its alif into a yā' since it changes in the second term, placing it in the position of a part, because the word indicates one referent, for kilā is the very thing it is attached to. This is unlike your saying thawbā al-rajulayn (the two garments of the two men) and farasā al-zaydayn (the two horses of the two Zaydes). If you said "marartu bi-kilā al-rajulayn" you would combine two signs of the dual in what is like one word, since they are never separated and this never leaves the annexation under any circumstances. Do you not see how they rejected "ḍarabtu ra'sī al-zaydayn" and said "ru'ūsuhumā" when they saw the annexed and the annexed-to as one noun? This is even though heads are often separated from annexation. Likewise the hearts in His saying ﴿ṣaghat qulūbukumā﴾ (your two hearts have inclined). If they rejected the sign of the dual there, although the annexation is incidental, then consider what it is in this position, where annexation never leaves it and is never separated from it. This is what led them to make its alif fixed in all cases, and this was better than the practice of Ṭayyi', Khath'am, Banū al-Ḥārith and others, who kept the alif of the dual in all cases, as in al-zaydān and al-ʿamrān, and when they annexed it to a pronoun, they turned its alif into a yā' in the accusative and genitive, because the pronoun has no sign of case and is not dualized with a yā' but always with an alif. Thus the reason they rejected appears to have ceased.

This view is the correct one, God willing, as you see, although Sībawayh is the greatest and foremost authority in the discipline; it is taken from his words and also left aside. What indicates the soundness of this view is that kilā is understood from its form what kull is understood from, and it agrees with it in the first radical and the middle radical. As for the final radical, it is deleted, as it is deleted in many nouns. So whoever claims that the final radical of the verb is a wāw and that it is not from the root of kull has no evidence supporting him and no derivation witnessing for him.

If it is said: "Why did the pronoun return to it in the singular form when it is dual?"

It is answered: because of the earlier-mentioned return of the pronoun to kull. This is an indication that the report concerns each one individually, as if you had said "kullu wāḥidin mina al-rajulayni qāma" (each one of the two men stood). There is a marvelous subtlety in it: returning the pronoun in the singular form is better, because it implies that the action proceeds from each one separately while also sharing it with the other.

If it is said: "Why was the kāf of kilā vowelled with a kasra when in kull it is vowelled with a ḍamma?"

It is answered: this is not binding on them, because they did not say that it is exactly the word kull. They may say that it was vowelled with a kasra to signal the meaning of duality, just as the word for two begins with a kasra. For this reason they vowelled the ʿayn of ʿishrīn (twenty) with a kasra, as a signal of the dual of ʿashar (ten). Another indication of the soundness of this view is that kiltā is equivalent to your saying thintā, and there is no disagreement that the alif of thintā is the alif of the dual, so likewise the alif of kiltā.

Whoever claims that its original form is kilawhumā has claimed what minds find far-fetched, and no proof supports it. Another indication of its soundness is that you say in emphasis "marartu bi-ikhwatika thalāthatihim wa arba'atihim" (I passed by your brothers, all three of them and all four of them), emphasizing with the number. Analogy would require that you say likewise for the dual, "marartu bi-akhawayka ithnayhimā," but they dispensed with it by using kilayhimā, because it has the same meaning, and if that is so, it is a dual like it.

If it is said: "You say kilā akhawayka jā'a (both your brothers came), and you do not say ithnā akhawayka jā'a (the two of your brothers came). This shows it does not have the same meaning."

It is answered: the number used as emphasis is only a delayed emphasis following what precedes it. When it is placed first, this is not permitted, because it has the sense of a qualifier, and a qualifier may not precede what it qualifies. So you do not say "thalāthatu ikhwatika jā'ūnī." This differs from kull, kilā and kiltā, because they contain the sense of encompassing, so they became like a particle entering upon a meaning that follows it. Hence it is good to place them first when reporting about them and to delay them when emphasizing. This is the position of this school, as you see.

**Chapter: On the Prophet's ﷺ guidance regarding what one says when seeing something in one's family or wealth that pleases him**

It is therefore fitting for whoever enters his garden or his house, or sees in his wealth and family something that pleases him, to hasten to this phrase, for then he will see nothing harmful in it.

On the authority of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"Allah does not bestow upon a servant a blessing in his family, his wealth, or his child, and he says: 'Whatever Allah wills (mā shā' Allāh), there is no power except through Allah (lā quwwata illā billāh),' except that he will see in it a calamity short of death."

And Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "Whatever Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"?﴾

And on his authority ﷺ, that when he saw something that gladdened him, he would say: "Praise be to Allah, by whose blessing good deeds are completed." And when he saw something that displeased him, he would say: "Praise be to Allah in every state."

**(Chapter: On a thing one sees and admires, and fears the evil eye for it)**

Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "Whatever Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"?﴾

The Prophet ﷺ said: "The evil eye is real; if anything could outrun the decree, the evil eye would outrun it." A sound hadith.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "If any of you sees in himself or in his wealth something that pleases him, let him invoke blessing upon it (fa-l-yatabarrak 'alayhi), for the evil eye is real."

It is also related from him ﷺ that he said: "Whoever sees something and is impressed by it, let him say: 'Whatever Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah.'"

It is also related from him ﷺ, concerning one who fears that something may be struck by his eye, that he said: "O Allah, bless it for us and do not let it come to harm."

Abu Sa'id said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to seek refuge from jinn and from the eye of man, until the two Mu'awwidhatayn (al-Mu'awwidhatayn, the last two surahs of the Qur'an) were revealed. When they were revealed, he took hold of them and abandoned whatever else."

Al-Tirmidhi said: a good hadith (hasan).

Ibn Majah narrated it in his Sunan.

**(Benefit)**

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever has many worries and griefs, let him increase in saying: 'There is no power nor strength except through Allah' (lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh)."

And it is established in the two Sahihs that it is a treasure from the treasures of Paradise.

**(Chapter)**

As for the effect of "There is no power nor strength except through Allah" in repelling this disease, [the burning of the heart, its distress, its concern and its sorrow], it is because of what it contains of complete reliance upon Allah, disavowal of any power or strength except through Him, surrender of the whole matter to Him, and not contending with Him over any part of it; and its generality covers every change from one state to another in the upper and lower worlds, and the capacity to effect that change; and that all of this is by Allah alone. Thus nothing can stand against this phrase.

In some reports it is stated that no angel descends from the heaven or ascends to it except with "There is no power nor strength except through Allah," and it has a wondrous effect in driving away Satan. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

**(Section)**

The indefinite noun (*nakirah*) in a negative context (*siyaq al-nafy*) denotes generality. This is derived from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾.

﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.

And in an interrogative context (*istifham*), from His words: ﴿Do you know of anyone equal to Him in name?﴾.

In a conditional context (*shart*), from His words: ﴿And if you see any human being﴾, and ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾.

And in a prohibition (*nahy*), from His words: ﴿And let none of you look back﴾.

And in an affirmative context (*ithbat*), by the generality of the general (*'umum al-'amma*) and by what is implied (*al-muqtada*), such as His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾.

And when it is attached to *kull* (every), as in: ﴿And every soul came﴾.

And from its generality by the generality of what is implied: ﴿And by a soul and He who proportioned it﴾.

This is the first part of Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 18, verse 50.

You have addressed this statement: I have been hostile to Iblis, I expelled him from My heaven and removed him from My nearness when he refused to prostrate to your father Adam. Then you, his descendants, take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me, though they are your enemies.

Let the intelligent person reflect on the placement of this address, on how strongly it clings to hearts and mingles with souls. Most of the Qur'an follows this manner of address to His servants, with affection, tenderness, kindness and far-reaching counsel. God, glorified is He, informs His servants that He does not desire for them anything but the noblest means, the best stations, and the most exalted knowledge and insight.

God, exalted is He, says:
﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed God is free of need of you, and He does not approve disbelief for His servants. But if you are grateful, He approves it for you.﴾ [Az-Zumar: 7]

He, exalted is He, says:
﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 3]

He says:
﴿God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 185]

He says:
﴿God intends to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise. God intends to turn to you in forgiveness, while those who follow their desires intend that you deviate into a great deviation. God intends to lighten for you, for man was created weak.﴾ [An-Nisa': 26-28]

(Section)

If it is said: What is the wisdom in the creation of Iblis and his hosts?

We say: In that there are wisdoms whose full detail none but God encompasses. Among them: that there be perfected for His prophets and friends the degrees of ʿubudiyya (servitude and worship) through striving against the enemy of God and his party, opposing them, defying them for the sake of God, enraging them and enraging His friends, seeking refuge in God from him, and turning to Him to protect them from his evil and his plotting. As a result there accrue to them worldly and otherworldly benefits that would not be attained without him. We have already mentioned that what depends upon a thing is not attained without it.

Among them: the fear of the angels and the believers of their own sin, after they witnessed what they witnessed of Iblis's condition and his fall from the angelic rank to the Iblisian state, becomes stronger and more complete. There is no doubt that when the angels witnessed that, there came to them another servitude toward the Lord, another submission and another fear, as is observed in the condition of a king's servants when they see that he has humiliated one of them with a humiliation that reached its utmost limit while they were watching. Without doubt their fear and caution become greater.

Among them: that He, glorified is He, made him a lesson for whoever opposes His command, is arrogant toward His obedience, and persists in His disobedience. Just as the sin of the father of humankind became a lesson for whoever commits what He forbade or disobeys His command and then repents, regrets and returns to his Lord. He tested the two fathers of jinn and mankind with sin: He made this father a lesson for whoever persists and remains in his sin, and that father a lesson for whoever repents and returns to his Lord.

So how many clear wisdoms and manifest signs are contained within that!

Among them: that He is a touchstone by which God tested His creation, so that the wicked among them might be distinguished from the good. He, glorified is He, created the human species from the earth, and in it there is the easy and the rough, the good and the wicked. So what was in its original substance necessarily appears in them, as in the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ):
"Indeed God created Adam from a handful He took from all the earth, so the children of Adam came in accordance with that: some of them good, some wicked, some easy, and some harsh."
And other than that.

What was in the original material exists in what is created from it. Divine wisdom therefore required its extraction and manifestation, and so there must be a cause that brings this out. Iblis was a touchstone by which the good is distinguished from the wicked, just as He made His prophets and messengers a touchstone for that distinction. God, exalted is He, says:
﴿God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good.﴾ [Al-Imran: 179]

He sent him to the responsible beings, among whom are the good and the wicked, so the good joins the good and the wicked joins the wicked. His perfect wisdom required that they be mixed together in the abode of trial. When they reach the abode of settlement, He distinguishes between them, and makes for these an abode apart and for those an abode apart: a perfect wisdom and an overwhelming power.

Among them: that the perfection of His power appears in creating the likes of Gabriel, the angels, Iblis and the devils. That is among the greatest of the signs of His power, will and sovereignty, for He is the creator of opposites: the heaven and the earth, the light and the darkness, Paradise and the Fire, water and fire, heat and cold, the good and the wicked.

Among them: that the creation of one of two opposites is part of the perfection of its opposite's beauty, for the opposite's goodness only appears through its opposite. Without ugliness, the excellence of beauty would not be known, and without poverty the worth of wealth would not be known, as has already been explained.

Among them: that He, glorified is He, loves to be thanked with the true reality of thanks and its various forms. Without doubt His friends obtained, through the existence of the enemy of God, Iblis and his hosts, and through being tested by them, kinds of gratitude that would not have been attained without them. How great is the difference between Adam's gratitude while he was in Paradise before he came out of it, and his gratitude after he was tested by his enemy, when his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness and accepted him.

Among them: that love, turning penitently to God, trust, patience, contentment and the like are the most beloved forms of servitude to God, glorified is He. This servitude is only realised through striving, giving oneself up for God, and placing His love above everything else. Striving is the summit of the hump of servitude and the most beloved of it to the Lord, glorified is He. So in the creation of Iblis and his party there is the establishment of the market of this servitude and its consequences, whose wisdoms and benefits and the interests in them none but God can count.

Among them: that in creating one who opposes His messengers, denies them and opposes them, there is part of the complete manifestation of His signs and the wonders of His power and the subtleties of His craftsmanship, which His existence makes more beloved to Him and more beneficial to His friends than its non-existence, as has been mentioned regarding the manifestation of the sign of the flood, the staff, the hand, the splitting of the sea, the casting of Abraham into the fire, and multiplications upon multiplications of His signs and proofs of His power, knowledge and wisdom. So there was no escape from the existence of the causes through which these results follow, as has been mentioned.

Among them: that the fiery substance contains burning, height and corruption, and it contains brightness, illumination and light. God, glorified is He, brought out both this and that from it, just as the earthly, dusty substance contains the good and the wicked, the easy and the rough, the red, the black and the white, and He brought out all of that from it: a perfect wisdom, an overwhelming power, and a sign indicating that ﴿there is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [Ash-Shura: 11].

Among them: that among His names are the Abaser, the Exalter, the Giver of honour, the Humiliator, the Wise, the Just, and the Avenger. These names require objects upon which their perfection appears, just as the names of Beneficence, Provision and Mercy and the like do. There must be the manifestation of the objects of these and of those.

Among them: that He, glorified is He, is the Complete Sovereign, and of the completeness of His sovereignty is the generality of His disposal and its variety through reward and punishment, honour and humiliation, justice and bounty, exaltation and debasement. So there must exist someone upon whom one of these two kinds is applied, just as He brought into existence someone upon whom the other kind is applied.

Among them: that among His names is the Wise, and wisdom is among His attributes, glorified is He. His wisdom requires placing everything in its proper place, which nothing else suits. So the creation of opposites required that each one be specialised with qualities, attributes and properties that suit none other than it. And is wisdom complete except by this? So the existence of this kind is part of the completeness of wisdom, just as it is part of the completeness of power.

Among them: that His praise, glorified is He, is complete and perfect from all aspects. He is praised for His justice, His withholding, His lowering, His vengeance and His humiliation, just as He is praised for His grace, His giving, His elevation and His honouring. So all perfect and complete praise belongs to God for this and for that. He praises Himself for all of that, and His angels, messengers and friends praise Him for it, and all the people of the Standing (on the Day of Judgement) praise Him for it. Whatever belongs to the completeness and perfection of His praise, He has in His creation and bringing into existence a perfect wisdom, just as He has the perfect praise. So it is not permissible to nullify His praise, just as it is not permissible to nullify His wisdom.

Among them: that He, glorified is He, loves to show His servants His forbearance, His patience, His clemency and the breadth of His mercy and generosity. That required the creation of one who associates others with Him, opposes Him in His judgement, strives to disobey Him and seeks what angers Him, indeed who likens Himself to Him, glorified is He. Yet He drives to him kinds of good things, provides for him, punishes him, enables him with the means of enjoying kinds of blessings, answers his supplication, removes evil from him, and deals with him in His goodness and kindness in the opposite manner to how he deals with Him through his disbelief, polytheism and wrongdoing.

How much wisdom and praise is in that! He makes Himself beloved to His friends and makes Himself known through kinds of His perfections, as in the authentic report from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said:
"None is more patient over harm he hears from God, when they attribute a son to Him, while He provides for them and pardons them."

In the authentic reports from the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated from his Lord:
"The son of Adam insults Me, and it is not fitting for him to do so; and the son of Adam denies Me, and it is not fitting for him to do so. As for his insulting Me, it is his saying: God has taken a son. And I am the One, the Eternal Refuge, who begets not, nor was begotten, and none is equal to Me. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: He will not restore me as He originated me, and the first creation is no easier for Him than its restoration."
Despite this insult and denial, He, glorified is He, provides for the one who insults and denies Him, punishes him, defends him, calls him to His Paradise, accepts his repentance if he turns to Him, replaces his evil deeds with good deeds, shows kindness to him in all his states, and qualifies him to be sent His messengers, and commands them to speak to him gently and to deal with him kindly.

Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said:
"There is no night whose darkness grows thick but the Majestic calls out, may His majesty be exalted: Who is more generous than Me? Creatures disobey Me, yet I watch over them in their beds as if they had not disobeyed Me, and I take charge of their protection as if they had not sinned. I am bountiful with grace toward the disobedient, and I show favour to the wrongdoer. Who has called upon Me and I have not answered him? Who has asked Me and I have not given him? I am the Bountiful, and generosity is from Me. I am the Generous, and generosity is from Me. And from My generosity is that I give the servant what he asks of Me, and I give him what he did not ask of Me. And from My generosity is that I give the penitent as if he had not disobeyed Me. Where do creatures flee from Me? And where do the disobedient turn away from My door?"

In a divine report: "I am, along with mankind and the jinn, in a great matter: I create while another is worshipped, I provide while another is thanked."

In a good report: "Son of Adam, you have not been just to Me. My good descends to you while your evil ascends to Me. I show you affection through blessings while I am independent of you, and you hate Me through acts of disobedience while you are needy of Me. The Noble Angel continues to ascend to Me with an ugly deed from you."

In the authentic hadith: "If you did not sin, God would take you away and bring a people who sin, then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them."

So He, glorified is He, because of the perfection of His love for His names and attributes, required by His praise and wisdom that He create a creation in whom their judgements and effects appear. Love for pardon is the creation of one toward whom pardon is shown well. Love for forgiveness is the creation of one whom He forgives, bears patiently with, and is patient toward; He does not hasten to punish him, but rather loves to grant him respite and delay. Love for His justice and wisdom is the creation of those in whom His justice and wisdom appear. Love for generosity, kindness and piety is the creation of those who deal with Him through evil and disobedience, while He deals with them through forgiveness and kindness. Without the creation of those through whose hands kinds of disobedience and transgressions occur, these wisdoms and benefits, and multiples upon multiples of them, would be lost.

Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds, the most wise of judges, possessor of perfect wisdom and abundant blessings, whose wisdom reaches as far as His power reaches. In everything He has a manifest wisdom, just as He has in it an overwhelming power and guidances. We have mentioned only a drop from the sea of them. Otherwise, human minds are too weak, too feeble and too short to encompass the perfection of His wisdom in any of His creation. How much has been achieved through this hateful creature, abhorred by the Lord and the object of His wrath, of what is beloved to Him, blessed and exalted is He, whose love connects with what has come from his hatefulness. The wise one of perfect wisdom is the one who achieves the more beloved of two matters by bearing the hardship he dislikes and which angers him, when it is a path to attaining that beloved; and the existence of what necessitates something without its consequence is impossible. If there has been achieved through the enemy of God, Iblis, joy and acts of disobedience, how much has been achieved through his existence and the existence of his hosts of obedience that is more beloved to God and more pleasing to Him than striving in His path and opposing the desire of the self and its appetite. And one bears hardships and hateful things for love of Him and seeking His pleasure. The most beloved thing to the beloved is that He sees His lover bear for His sake harm and hardship that proves his love:

"For your sake I made my cheek a ground
For the mocker and the envious, until you are pleased."

In a divine report: "My desire is what those who endure bear for My sake."

How beloved to Him is the endurance of His lovers when His enemies harm them for His sake and seeking His pleasure! How beneficial that harm is to them! How praiseworthy they are for its outcome! What honour they gain from their Beloved, and how the nearness to Him becomes the coolness of their eyes! But it is forbidden for those who deny the love of the Lord, exalted is He, to smell any fragrance of it, enter by this door, or taste this drink:

"Say to the blind eyes: the sun has eyes
other than yours, which see it at its setting and its rising."

"And pardon the wretch who has not been qualified for His love,
for specification is not fitting in every place."

If this creature angers his Lord, then He is pleased by what His prophets, messengers and friends do in it, and that pleasure is greater than that anger. If the acts of disobedience and transgressions that occur through his hands displease Him, then He, glorified is He, is more joyful at the repentance of His servant than one who has lost his mount, upon which is his food and drink, and finds it in deadly deserts. If what took place against His prophets and messengers by this enemy angers Him, then what took place at their hands of fighting him, disobeying him, opposing him, humbling him and enraging him has pleased and satisfied Him. That pleasure is greater with Him and more honourable to Him than the loss of that hateful thing, which entails the loss of this pleased and beloved thing. If Adam's eating from the tree displeased Him, then his repentance, return, submission, humbling before Him and brokenness before Him has pleased Him. If the expulsion of His messenger from his sanctuary and his city by his enemies angered Him, then, due to that expulsion alone, his entering it in that manner pleased Him the greatest pleasure. If the killing of His friends and beloved, the tearing of their flesh and the spilling of their blood displeased Him, then their attaining the life that is no better, no more pleasant and no sweeter, in His nearness and His neighbourhood, has pleased Him. If the acts of disobedience of His servants displease Him, then the witnessing by His angels, prophets, messengers and friends of the breadth of His forgiveness, His pardon, His kindness, His generosity and His bounty, and the praise of Him for these qualities, and their glorifying Him with the attributes by which He praised Himself and was praised, is more beloved to Him and more pleasing to Him than the loss of those acts of disobedience and the loss of these beloved things.

Know that praise is the comprehensive root of all of that. It is the bond of the order of creation and command. The Lord, exalted is He, has all praise in all its aspects, considerations and turnings. He has not created anything nor judged anything except that He has praise in it. So His praise reaches as far as His creation reaches. And His command is praise in truth, comprising His love, His contentment with it and from it, His praise of it, and the affirmation of His perfect wisdom in all He created and commanded. So nullifying His wisdom is different from nullifying His praise, as has been explained. Just as He is not except praiseworthy, He is not except wise. His praise and His wisdom, like His knowledge, power and life, are among the necessities of His essence, and it is not permissible to nullify any of His attributes and names from their requirements and effects, for that would entail the deficiency that contradicts His perfection, His greatness and His majesty.

The twenty-fifth aspect: just as among the attributes of perfection and actions deserving praise and commendation is that He is generous, gives and bestows, among them is that He grants refuge, victory and relief. Just as He loves that those who seek refuge in Him turn to Him, He loves that those who take refuge in Him seek His protection. The perfection of kings is that their friends seek refuge with them and take shelter in them, as al-Ahmad ibn Husayn al-Kindi said about his patron:

"O you to whom I turn for what I hope for,
and in whom I seek refuge from what I fear.
No people mend a bone you have broken,
and no people break a bone you have set."

Had he said this about his Lord and Creator, it would have been more fortunate for him than saying it about a creature like himself. The point is that the King of kings loves that His servants seek refuge in Him and take shelter in Him, as He commanded His Messenger to seek refuge in Him from the accursed Satan in more than one place in His Book. By this the completeness of His blessing upon His enemy appears, when He grants him refuge and protects him from his enemy, and the granting of refuge and protection from him is not the lesser of the two blessings. God, exalted is He, loves to perfect His blessing upon His believing servants and to show them His victory over their enemy, His protection of them from him, and their triumph over him. How great a blessing it is by which their joy and bliss are perfected, and a justice He manifests against His enemies and opponents:

"And between them, God has a wisdom
that every seeker falls short of comprehending."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 18, verse 50 (part 2 of 2):

Among the greatest of its punishments is that it necessitates severance between the servant and his Lord, blessed and exalted is He. When severance occurs, the causes of good are cut off from him and the causes of evil are joined to him. So what success is there, what hope, and what life is there for one from whom the causes of good have been cut off, who has severed what is between him and his Protector and Master, without whom he cannot be independent even for the blink of an eye, for whom there is no substitute and no replacement, and the causes of evil have been joined to him, and what is between him and his greatest enemy has been connected, so that his enemy takes charge of him and his Protector abandons him? No soul knows what kinds of pains and what kinds of torment are in this severance and this connection.

One of the early pious predecessors (al-salaf) said: "I saw the servant placed between Allah, glorified is He, and Satan. If Allah turns away from him, Satan takes charge of him; and if Allah takes charge of him, Satan cannot prevail over him." And the Exalted has said: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾

He, glorified is He, says to His servants: "I honored your father, raised his rank, and preferred him over others. So I commanded all My angels to prostrate to him, as honor and distinction for him. They obeyed Me, but My enemy and his enemy refused, disobeyed My command, and departed from My obedience. How, then, is it fitting for you, after this, to take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, obeying him in disobedience to Me and befriending him in opposition to what pleases Me, while they are your greatest enemy? You have befriended My enemy when I had commanded you to oppose him." Whoever befriends the enemies of the king is, in the king's sight, the same as those enemies, for love and obedience are not complete except by opposing the enemies of the one obeyed and befriending his allies. As for befriending the enemies of the king while claiming to be loyal to him, that is impossible.

This would be so even if the king's enemy were not your enemy; how much more so when he is truly your enemy, and the enmity between you and him is greater than the enmity between the sheep and the wolf? How, then, is it proper for an intelligent person to befriend his enemy, the enemy of his Protector and Master, besides whom he has no master? He, glorified is He, pointed out the ugliness of this befriending by His saying: ﴿while they are an enemy to you﴾, just as He pointed out its ugliness by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿he departed from the command of his Lord﴾.
