Thus it becomes clear that his enmity toward his Lord and his enmity toward us are each a cause that calls for opposing him. So what is this befriending? And what is this substitution? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.

It may be that beneath this address there is a kind of gentle and wondrous reproach, namely: "I opposed Iblis when he did not prostrate to your father Adam along with My angels, so his opposition was on your account. Then the outcome of this opposition was that you concluded between yourselves and him a treaty of reconciliation."

(Exhortation)

O you who are among the people of insight, have you come to know the worth of yourself? Indeed, all the worlds were created for you.
O you who were nourished with the milk of piety and whose heart is in the hands of subtle kindnesses:
All things are a tree, and you are the fruit;
a form, and you are the meaning;
a shell, and you are the pearl;
a churn, and you are the butter.
The manifest of our choosing you is clear in its script, but your extraction of it is weak.
When you seek My pursuit, then seek Me in yourself.
Woe to you! If you had known your own worth, you would not have degraded it with sins.
We only expelled Iblis because he did not prostrate to you, while you were in your father's loins.
How strange! How did you make peace with him and abandon us: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾
If there were love in your heart, its effect would have appeared upon your body.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 18, verse 57:

It is the plural of kinan (kinān), like ʿinān and aʿinna (reins). Its root meaning is covering and concealment.

It is said: kanahu, akannahu, and kinān (with the same sense), though there is in fact a difference between them. Akannahu means he concealed it and hid it.

As in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Or you conceal it within yourselves﴾ (Qur'an 2:235). Kannahu means he preserved and guarded it, as in His words: ﴿As if they were eggs well-guarded﴾ (Qur'an 37:49). The two share the sense of covering.

Al-kinān (kinān) is that which conceals a thing and covers it; it is like a sheath.

They themselves acknowledged this about themselves, saying: ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you invite us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier﴾ (Qur'an 41:5).

So they mentioned the covering of the heart, which is the akinna (coverings); the covering of the ear, which is the waqr (deafness); and the covering of the eye, which is the hijab (barrier).

The meaning is: we do not understand your speech, we do not hear it, and we do not see you.

The meaning is also: in refusing to accept from you, we are in the position of one who does not understand what you say and does not see you.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Our hearts are under coverings" means like the quiver (kinānah) in which the arrows are kept.

Mujahid said: like the case of the arrows (jaʿbat al-nabl).

Muqatil said: there is a covering over them, so we do not understand what you say.

(Benefit)

When Musa set out to al-Khidr, he found on his journey hunger and fatigue, so he said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have met with fatigue from this journey of ours﴾

For this was a journey to a created being.

And when his Lord appointed him thirty nights and completed them with ten, he did not eat during them, and he did not find the touch of hunger or fatigue, for this was a journey to his Lord, exalted is He.

Likewise, the journey of the heart and its progress toward its Lord: it does not find in it the hardship and weariness that one finds in journeying to some created beings.

**[Section: The Station of Knowledge]**

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of knowledge.

If this station does not accompany the wayfarer from the first step he takes on the path until the last step he reaches, then his journey is off the path. The road to arrival is cut off for him, the ways of guidance and success are blocked to him, and their doors are closed to him. This is the consensus of the knowing shaykhs. Only the highwaymen among them, and the deputies and agents of Iblis, have forbidden knowledge.

The master and shaykh of the Sufi order, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "All paths are blocked to creation except for the one who follows the footsteps of the Messenger (ﷺ)."

He also said: "Whoever has not memorized the Qur'an and written down the hadith should not be followed in this matter, because our knowledge is bound by the Book and the Sunnah."

He also said: "Our way is bound by the principles of the Book and the Sunnah."

Abu Hafs, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Whoever does not weigh his actions and states at all times by the Book and the Sunnah, and does not distrust his own inspirations, is not counted among the men (of worth)."

Abu Sulayman al-Darani, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Sometimes a subtle insight from the insights of the people comes into my heart for days. I accept it only with two just witnesses: the Book and the Sunnah."

Sahl ibn Abdullah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Every act that the servant performs without following a model, whether obedience or disobedience, is a life for the self (i.e., indulgence of the self). And every act that the servant performs by following a model is a torment for the self."

al-Sarri said: "Sufism is a name for three meanings: his light of knowledge is not extinguished by the light of his scrupulousness; he does not speak of an esoteric matter in knowledge that the outward meaning of the Book contradicts; and miraculous gifts do not lead him to tear down the veils over what Allah has forbidden."

Abu Yazid said: "I struggled (in discipline) for thirty years, and I found nothing harder on me than knowledge and following it. Had it not been for the disagreement of the scholars, I would have remained (in my state). The disagreement of the scholars is a mercy, except regarding the purification of tawhid."

He once said to his servant: "Come, let us go to this man who has advertised himself as righteous, so that we may visit him." When they entered the mosque together, the man spat and threw it toward the qiblah. Abu Yazid turned back without greeting him, and said: "This man is not trustworthy in one of the manners of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); how can he be trustworthy in what he claims?"

He also said: "I was determined to ask Allah, exalted is He, to spare me the burden of women. Then I said: How is it permissible for me to ask Allah for this, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not ask it, and I have not asked it?"

"Then Allah spared me the burden of women, to the extent that I do not care whether a woman or a wall meets me."

He also said: "If you see a man given miraculous gifts to the point of rising into the air, do not be deceived by him until you see how you find him in (matters of) commanding and forbidding, guarding the limits (set by Allah), and performing the Shari'ah."

Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Whoever does a deed without following the Sunnah, his deed is void."

Abu Uthman al-Nisaburi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Companionship with Allah is through good manners, constant awe, and vigilance. Companionship with the Messenger (ﷺ) is through following his Sunnah and adhering to the outward knowledge. Companionship with the friends of Allah is through respect and service. Companionship with family is through good character. Companionship with brothers is through constant cheerfulness, so long as it is not sinful. Companionship with the ignorant is through supplicating for them and showing them mercy."

Another (scholar) added: "Companionship with the two recording angels is through honoring and respecting them, and dictating to them what will make them praise you. Companionship with the self is through opposing it. Companionship with Satan is through enmity."

Abu Uthman also said: "Whoever makes the Sunnah a ruler over himself in word and deed speaks with wisdom, and whoever makes his desire a ruler over himself in word and deed speaks with innovation." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾ [al-Nur: 54].

Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri said: "Whoever you see claiming, with Allah, exalted and majestic is He, a state that takes him beyond the limits of the Shari'i knowledge, do not go near him."

Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Balkhi, one of the great shaykhs of the people, said: "Islam is lost through four (things): they do not act upon what they know, they act upon what they do not know, they do not learn what they act upon, and they prevent people from learning and teaching."

Amr ibn Uthman al-Makki said: "Knowledge is the leader, and fear is the driver, while the self is a balky (stubborn) animal in between: it is headstrong, deceptive, and evasive. So beware of it, and manage it with the policy of knowledge, and drive it with the threat of fear, and what you desire will be accomplished for you."

Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz said: "Every inward matter that the outward contradicts is false."

Ibn Ata said: "Whoever binds his self to the manners of the Sunnah, Allah illuminates his heart with the light of gnosis."

"There is no station more noble than the station of following the Beloved in his commands, actions, and character."

He also said: "Whatever you ask about, seek it in the expanse of knowledge. If you do not find it there, then in the field of wisdom. If you do not find it there, then weigh it by tawhid. If you do not find it in these three places, then strike it in the face of Satan."

Banan the porter was thrown before a predatory beast, which began to sniff him without harming him. When he was taken out, he was asked: "What was in your heart when the beast sniffed you?" He said: "I was reflecting on the scholars' disagreement about the leftover water of predatory animals."

Abu Hamza al-Baghdadi, one of the great shaykhs (and Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to say to him in questions: "What do you say, O Sufi?"), said: "Whoever knows the path of truth, its traversing becomes easy for him. There is no guide to the path to Allah except following the Messenger (ﷺ) in his states, sayings, and actions."

Shaykh Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Musa al-Wasiti passed on a Friday on his way to the congregational mosque, and the thong of his sandal broke. A pharmacist repaired it for him. He said: "Do you know why my sandal thong broke?" I said: "No." He said: "Because I have not bathed for the Friday prayer." He then asked: "Is there a bathhouse here that you enter?" He said: "Yes." So he entered and bathed.

Abu Ishaq al-Raqqi, a contemporary of al-Junayd, said: "The sign of the love of Allah is: preferring His obedience, and following His Messenger (ﷺ)."

Abu Ya'qub al-Nahrajuri said: "The best states are those accompanied by knowledge."

Abu al-Qasim al-Nasrabadhi, shaykh of Khurasan in his time, said: "The foundation of Sufism is: adhering to the Book and the Sunnah; abandoning desires and innovations; honoring the miracles of the shaykhs; seeing the excuses of creation; persisting in the litanies; and abandoning the pursuit of concessions and far-fetched interpretations."

Abu Bakr al-Tamistani, one of the great shaykhs of the order, said: "The path is clear, and the Book and the Sunnah stand among us."

The virtue of the Companions is well known, due to their precedence in emigration and their companionship (with the Prophet). Whoever keeps company with the Book and the Sunnah, becomes a stranger to his self and to creation, and emigrates in his heart to Allah, he is the truthful and correct one.

Abu Amr ibn Nujayd said: "Every state that does not result from knowledge, its harm to its possessor is greater than its benefit."

He also said: "Sufism is patience under the commands and prohibitions."

Some of the great early shaykhs used to say: "O company of Sufis, do not abandon the black (of the letters) for the white (of the paper), lest you perish."

**[The Excellence and Virtue of Knowledge]**

As for the sayings that are reported from some of them that discourage seeking knowledge and deem oneself independent of it, such as the saying of one who said: "We take our knowledge from the Living One who does not die, while you take yours from one who dies";

and the saying of another, when it was said to him: "Will you not travel to hear from ʿAbd al-Razzaq?" He replied: "What use is hearing from ʿAbd al-Razzaq to one who hears from the Creator?";

and the saying of another: "Knowledge is a veil between the heart and Allah, exalted and majestic is He";

and the saying of another: "We have the knowledge of the letter, and you have the knowledge of the paper";

and similar sayings whose best interpretation for their speakers is that they are ignorant and excused by their ignorance, or ecstatic utterers who acknowledge their ecstasy. Otherwise, were it not for ʿAbd al-Razzaq and his like, and were it not for "He informed us" and "He narrated to us," not a single part of Islam would have reached us, nor would it have reached this (person) or his like.

Whoever refers you to something other than "He informed us" and "He narrated to us," has referred you either to the imagination of a Sufi, the analogy of a philosopher, or personal opinion. There is nothing after the Qur'an and "He informed us" and "He narrated to us" except the doubts of the theologians, the opinions of deviators, the imaginings of Sufis, and the analogies of philosophers. Whoever departs from the proof strays from the right path. There is no proof to Allah and Paradise except the Book and the Sunnah. Every path that is not accompanied by the proof of the Qur'an and the Sunnah is one of the paths of Hellfire and of the accursed Satan.

Knowledge is that which is established by proof, and the beneficial part of it is that which the Messenger brought.

Knowledge is superior to state: knowledge is the judge, and state is what is judged. Knowledge is the guide, and state is the follower. Knowledge is the commander and forbidder.

State is a receptive channel, and state is a sword: if it is not accompanied by knowledge, it is a toy sword in the hand of a player.

State is a mount that cannot be overtaken; if it is not accompanied by knowledge, it throws its rider into perils and destruction.

State is like wealth, which is given to both the righteous and the wicked. If it is not accompanied by the light of knowledge, it becomes a burden upon its possessor.

State without knowledge is like a ruler whom no restraint holds back from his tyranny.

State without knowledge is like a fire that has no one to manage it.

The benefit of state does not extend beyond its possessor, while the benefit of knowledge is like rain that falls on the hills, the mounds, the valley floors, and the places where trees grow.

The circle of knowledge encompasses this world and the Hereafter, while the circle of state is too narrow for anyone other than its possessor, and may sometimes be too narrow even for him.

Knowledge is the guide, and sound state is guided by it. It is the inheritance and legacy of the Prophets. Its people are their kinsmen and heirs. It is the life of hearts, the light of insights, the healing of breasts, the gardens of minds, the delight of souls, the companion of the lonely, and the guide of the bewildered.

It is the balance by which sayings, deeds, and states are weighed.

It is the judge that distinguishes between doubt and certainty, between error and right guidance, and between guidance and misguidance.

By it Allah is known and worshipped, remembered and declared One, praised and glorified. By it the wayfarers were guided to Him, and through its path the arrivers arrived, and through its gate the seekers entered upon Him.

By it the laws and rulings are known, and the lawful is distinguished from the unlawful. By it family ties are maintained, and by knowing and following the pleasures of the Beloved, one reaches Him from near.

It is the imam, and deeds are its followers. It is the leader, and deeds are its followers. It is the companion in strangeness, the one who speaks with you in solitude, the friend in loneliness, the one who uncovers doubt, the wealth that brings no poverty to whoever attains its treasure, and the shelter that brings no ruin to whoever takes refuge in its protection.

Its remembrances are glorification; seeking it is jihad; seeking it is nearness; giving it away is charity; studying it equals fasting and night prayer; and the need for it is greater than the need for drink and food.

Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "People need knowledge more than they need food and drink, because a man needs food and drink once or twice a day, while his need for knowledge is as many as his breaths."

It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Seeking knowledge is better than voluntary prayer."

Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, also explicitly stated this.

Ibn Wahb said: "I was before Malik, may Allah be pleased with him. I put down my writing tablets and stood to pray. He said: 'What you stood up to is not better than what you left.'"

Ibn Abd al-Barr and others mentioned this.

Allah, exalted and majestic is He, called upon the people of knowledge as witnesses to the most exalted thing to be witnessed, which is tawhid, and joined their testimony with His own and that of His angels. Implicit in this is their being declared trustworthy, for He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, does not call as a witness one who is discredited.

From this point, Allah knows best, the well-known hadith is derived: "This knowledge will be carried by the trustworthy of every generation, who will remove from it the distortion of the extremists, the false interpretation of the falsifiers."

It is the proof of Allah on His earth, His light among His servants, their leader and guide to His Paradise, and the one who brings them near to His honor.

Part 2 of the commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 18, verse 65:

It is sufficient for its honour that the superiority of its people over the servants is like the superiority of the full moon on the night of the full moon over all the other stars. And that the angels lower their wings for them and shade them with them, and that the scholar is asked forgiveness by whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, even the fish in the sea, and even the ant in its hole. And that Allah and His angels send blessings upon those who teach people good.

Moses ibn Imran, the one whom Allah the Merciful spoke to directly (upon him be prayers and peace), travelled in pursuit of knowledge, he and his young companion, until fatigue touched them both on their journey in pursuit of knowledge, until he obtained three matters.

He is among the most honoured of creation before Allah and the most knowledgeable of them concerning Him.

Allah commanded His Messenger to ask Him for more of it, and He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114].

Allah forbade the hunting of ignorant hunting animals, and He only permitted for the community the hunting of knowledgeable hunting animals.

Thus, the faculties of the ignorant person, his hunting by them of deeds, benefit him nothing. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best.

[Chapter: The definition of knowledge]

Chapter

The author of "al-Manazil" (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Knowledge is that which is established by evidence and removes ignorance.

He means: knowledge has a sign before it and a sign after it. Its sign before it is that which evidence has established. Its sign after it is the removal of ignorance.

[The degrees of knowledge]

[The first degree: manifest knowledge]

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: manifest knowledge ('ilm jali), by which direct witnessing occurs, and sound widespread report (istifadah sahihah), or the soundness of an old experiment.

He means by the manifest: the apparent, which has no concealment. He made it three kinds.

The first of them: that which occurs through direct sight. This is the sight.

The second: that which rests on hearing. This is the knowledge of widespread report (ilm al-istifadah).

The third: that which rests on the intellect. This is the knowledge of experiment (ilm al-tajribah).

These three paths, namely hearing, sight and intellect, are the paths of knowledge and its gates, and the paths of knowledge are not confined to what he mentioned. For all the other senses produce knowledge.

Likewise, that which is perceived inwardly, which is the intuitive matters (al-wijdaniyyat).

Likewise, that which is perceived through the report of a truthful informant, even if he is one person.

Likewise, that which is attained through reflection and inference, even if it does not come from experiment.

Knowledge therefore is not restricted to these three alone.

The difference between it and gnosis (ma'rifah) lies in three respects.

The first: gnosis is the core (lubb) of knowledge, and the relation of knowledge to it is like the relation of faith to excellence (ihsan). It is a specific knowledge whose object is more hidden and more subtle than the object of knowledge.

The second: gnosis is the knowledge which its possessor observes in accordance with its requirement and its demand. It is knowledge to which observance is joined.

The third: gnosis is a witness in itself, and it is like the intuitive matters, which its possessor cannot doubt and does not move away from.

The unveiling of gnosis is more complete than the unveiling of knowledge. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best.

[Chapter: The second degree: hidden knowledge]

Chapter

He said: The second degree: hidden knowledge ('ilm khafi). It grows in pure secrets, from purified bodies, by the water of sincere discipline, and it appears in sincere breaths, for the people of lofty resolve, in the empty moments and the attentive ears. It is knowledge that makes the absent manifest, makes the witnessed disappear, and points to the unity (al-jam').

He means: this knowledge is hidden from the people of the first degree, and it is what this group call gnosis.

His words: it grows in pure secrets.

The word "sirr" (secret) is used in their language and they intend several things by it.

The first: the subtle essence deposited in this frame, by which perception, love, will and knowledge are attained. That is the spirit (ruh).

The second: a meaning subsisting in the spirit, whose relation to the spirit is like the relation of the spirit to the body.

Often they mean by it this meaning.

Among them: the heart is the most noble part of the body, the spirit is more noble than the heart, and the secret (sirr) is subtler than the spirit.

Among them also: the secret has another secret, which none knows but the Real, glory be to Him. Its possessor does not comprehend it, even if he comprehends his secret. So they say: "The secret is that over which you have no oversight, and the secret of the secret is that which none has knowledge of except the Real, glory be to Him."

The third meaning: it is used for what is kept protected and hidden between the servant and his Lord, of states and stations. As one of them said: "Our secrets are virgin; no delusion of a deluded person has deflowered them." And their speaker says: "If my button knew my secret, I would throw it away."

The intended meaning of his words: it grows in pure secrets.

He means: pure from the turbidity of this world and occupation with it, and its attachments which hinder the spirits from the abodes of joy.

For these are turbidities and breaths upon the face of the mirror of the heart and the spirit, so the forms of realities do not clearly appear in it as they should. And the soul breathes upon it constantly with desire for this world and fear of losing it.

When the mirror is polished by removing these turbidities, it becomes clear, and realities and gnoses appear in it.

As for the purified bodies:

They are those purified by obedience to Allah, and grown upon the eating of what is lawful. When bodies are freed from what is unlawful and from the filth of humanity which reason, religion and manliness forbid, and souls are purified from the attachments of this world, the land of the heart becomes pure, and it accepts the seed of knowledges and gnoses. If it is then watered by the water of the legislated, prophetic, Muhammadan discipline, which does not depart from knowledge, does not stray from an obligation, and does not neglect a sunnah, it brings forth from every noble pair knowledge, wisdom, benefit and recognition. Its possessor and whoever sits with him gather from it kinds of rarities and benefits, and fruits of varied colours and tastes, as one of the early generations said: "When hearts are bound to abandoning sins, they roam in the malakut, and then return to their owners with kinds of gifts and benefits."

His words: and it appears in sincere breaths. By breaths he means two things.

The first: breaths of remembrance and gnosis.

The second: breaths of love and will, and what is connected to the known object and the beloved desired by the one who remembers and the lover. Their sincerity is their purity from the admixtures of others and of personal portions.

His words: for the people of lofty resolve. These are the resolves that do not stop short of Allah, mighty and majestic, and do not turn aside on their journey to anything other than Him. The highest resolve is that which is attached to the Most High. The broadest is that which is attached to the welfare of the servants. These are the resolves of the Messengers, prayers and peace of Allah be upon them, and of their heirs.

His words: in the empty moments.

He means by them: the hours of clarity with Allah, Exalted, and the times of divine breezes, whoever exposes himself to them is close to not being deprived of them, and whoever turns away from them, they turn away from him even more.

His words: in the attentive ears.

These are the ears that are cleansed from attachment to falsehood and idle talk, and that listen to the call of truth and the herald of faith. For falsehood and idle talk are the wine of ears and minds, so their sobriety is by avoiding it and listening to the call of truth.

His words: it makes the absent manifest, that is, it uncovers what was absent from the knower.

His words: and makes the witnessed disappear, that is, it makes him disappear from witnessing anything other than the witnessed Real.

And it points to the unity (al-jam'), which is the station of singularity and the effacement of traces, even the trace of the witness himself. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best.

[Chapter: The third degree: divinely bestowed knowledge]

Chapter

He said: The third degree: divinely bestowed knowledge ('ilm ladunni). Its ascription is its existence, its perception is its direct witnessing, its description is its judgment. Between it and the Unseen there is no veil.

The people intend by divinely bestowed knowledge that which the servant attains without an intermediary, rather by inspiration from Allah and His making it known to His servant, as happened to Khidr, upon him be peace, without the intermediary of Moses. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We gave him mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

He distinguished between the mercy and the knowledge, and made both "from Us" (min 'indina) and "from Our presence" (min ladunna), since he did not receive them through the hand of a human; and "from Our presence" is more particular and closer than "from Us". For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sincere entrance and bring me out a sincere exit, and grant me from Yourself a helping authority﴾ [al-Isra: 80]. So the helping authority from His presence, glory be to Him, is more particular and closer than what is "from Him".

For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and grant me from Yourself a helping authority﴾ [al-Isra: 80].

And it is that with which He strengthened him. What is "from Him" is His aid through the believers, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He it is who strengthened you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 62].

Divinely bestowed knowledge is the fruit of servanthood and following, of sincerity with Allah, of devotion to Him, and of striving to receive knowledge from the niche of His Messenger, and of perfect submission to him. Then He opens to him from the understanding of the Book and the Sunnah by a matter specific to him, as ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said when he was asked whether the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had singled them out with anything apart from the people: "No, by Him who split the grain and created the soul, except an understanding which Allah gives a servant in His Book."

This is the true divinely bestowed knowledge. As for the knowledge of one who turns away from the Book and the Sunnah and does not bind himself to them, it comes from the presence of the self, desire and Satan, and is thus "divinely bestowed" too, but from whose presence? The knowledge is known to be divinely bestowed and merciful only by its agreement with what the Messenger ﷺ brought from his Lord, mighty and majestic.

Divinely bestowed knowledge is therefore of two kinds: a merciful divinely bestowed knowledge, and a satanic, belly-born divinely bestowed knowledge. The touchstone is revelation, and there is no revelation after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for the story of Moses with Khidr, peace be upon them both: to cite it to permit dispensing with revelation through divinely bestowed knowledge is heresy and disbelief that takes one out of Islam and makes the shedding of blood obligatory.

The difference is that Moses was not sent to Khidr, and Khidr was not commanded to follow him. Had he been commanded to, it would have been obligatory for him to migrate to Moses and be with him. For this reason he said to him: "Are you Moses, the prophet of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes."

Muhammad ﷺ was sent to all of the two categories (jinn and mankind). His message is general to the jinn and mankind, in every age. Had Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, been alive, they would have been among his followers, and when Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon them both, descends, he will only judge by the law of Muhammad ﷺ.

Therefore whoever claims that he is with Muhammad ﷺ as Khidr was with Moses, or permits that for anyone of the community, let him renew his Islam and pronounce the testimony of truth, for by that he has wholly departed from the religion of Islam, let alone being one of the special friends of Allah. He is rather one of the friends of Satan, his successors and his deputies.

This point is a dividing line and a separation between the heretics of this group and the upright among them, so examine its trace (fa-harrik tarahu).

His words: its ascription is its existence.

He means: the way to this knowledge is direct finding (wijdan), just as the way to other knowledge is ascription (isnad).

Its perception is its direct witnessing: that is, this knowledge is not taken by reflection and inference, but is taken by direct witnessing and contemplation.

Its description is its judgment. He means: its attributes cannot be reached except through it, and its attributes fall short of it. That is, its witness is from it and it is the proof of its existence; its "that" (innīyah) is its "why" (lammīyah), so the proof of the "that" in it is the proof of the "why". It is both the evidence and the thing evidenced. For this reason there is no veil between it and the unseen, unlike the knowledge beneath it, between which and the sciences there is a veil.

What the people point to is a light from the presence of the Witnessed, which effaces the powers of the senses and their rulings, and stands in the place of them for its possessor. It is witnessed by its light, and everything else perishes by its manifestation. This, in their view, is the meaning of the divine trace: "When I love him, I become his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees... so by Me he hears, and by Me he sees."

Merciful divinely bestowed knowledge is the fruit of this agreement and the love that is produced by drawing near through supererogatory acts after obligatory ones.

Satanic divinely bestowed knowledge is the fruit of turning away from revelation and making desire and Satan the judge. And Allah is the One sought for help.

As for His words, ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾: if the reading "and there was before them a king" (wa-kana amamahum malik) is sound, then it has a meaning that does not contradict the common reading. That is, the king was behind them (as they set out), and their return was toward him, so he was behind them in their going and before them in their returning. Thus both readings hold with respect to these two considerations. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best.

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after a lengthy discussion of Imam Ahmad's (may Allah have mercy on him) interpretation of the fitrah (innate disposition) and what follows from it:

As for the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) concerning the boy whom al-Khidr killed, that "he was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever," the same applies.

"Kafiran" (as a disbeliever) is a future-situational circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), not a simultaneous one (hal muqarinah). That is, he was sealed with his disbelief destined, for otherwise, while he was in the womb and a child who does not understand, he was neither a disbeliever nor a believer.

If it is said: If this is so, why did al-Khidr kill him? The answer is what he said to Musa: ﴿And I did it not of my own accord﴾ [al-Kahf: 82]. Allah the Exalted commanded him to kill that boy for a benefit, and He commanded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to refrain from killing women and children (dhurriyyah) for a benefit. So in everything He commands there is a benefit, wisdom and mercy witnessed by people of understanding (ulu al-albab).

Then he said:

As for his saying, "The boy whom al-Khidr killed was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever," what is meant by it is that he was written and sealed (kutiba wa khutima). The word "tab'" (sealing/stamping), since many people use it for "tabi'ah" (natural temperament), which means disposition and innate nature, the one who thinks so supposed that this is what the hadith means.

This boy whom al-Khidr killed may have been an adult in absolute terms, and was called "ghulam" (boy) because of the closeness of his time to puberty; in that case there is no difficulty. It may also be that he was a discerning, intelligent child (mumayyiz 'aqil), though not yet an adult, and the hadith indicates this, namely his saying: "Had he reached adulthood he would have burdened his parents (arhaqa abawayhi)." In that case there is nothing to prevent him from being accountable (mukallaf) under that earlier law, since making puberty a condition of accountability is only a rule of our sharia, and there is nothing impossible in the rational obligation of a discerning intelligent youth. Indeed, a number of scholars have said that discerning children are obligated to believe before reaching puberty (ihtilam), as a group of the companions of Abu Hanifah and Ahmad said, and it is the view chosen by Abu al-Khattab, and a group of the theologians (ahl al-kalam) also held it.

On this basis, it is possible that this boy was accountable for belief before puberty, even if he was not accountable for the (detailed) laws. The disbelief of a discerning child is considered valid according to most scholars; so if he apostatized according to them, he becomes an apostate with the rulings of apostates, although he is not to be killed until he reaches puberty, and then his disbelief is confirmed against him. They agreed that he is to be beaten and disciplined for his disbelief more severely than for abandoning prayer. If the boy whom al-Khidr killed was an adult, there is no difficulty; and if he was a discerning youth not yet adult, his killing was permissible under that law, because he killed him by the command of Allah. How much more so, since he killed him only to repel his assault upon his parents in religion, as He said: ﴿So We feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾ [al-Kahf: 80]. If a child attacked a Muslim in his body or property, and his aggression could not be repelled from the Muslim except by killing him, it is permissible to kill him; indeed, if a child fights Muslims, he is killed. But how is it known that this child today will attack his parents or others in their religion so as to seduce them away from it? This is an unseen matter for which we have no way of knowledge. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas made the ruling depend on it, when Najdah asked him about killing children, and he said:

"If you know from them what al-Khidr knew about that boy, then kill them; otherwise, do not."

Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih.

But it may be said: The principle of the sharia and of recompense is that Allah the Glorified does not punish His servants for what He knows they will do; rather He does not punish them except after they have done what they know He forbade, and He warned them in advance of punishment for doing it. The story of al-Khidr contains nothing of knowledge of the unseen that none knows but Allah; it contains only his knowledge of causes that necessitate their rulings. Musa did not know those causes, such as al-Khidr's knowledge that the ship belonged to poor people and that behind them was a tyrannical king who would seize any sound ship; so making a hole in it was to save it entirely, then it would be restored, one of the best rulings, and it is the repelling of the greater of two evils by accepting the lesser of them. On this basis, if a person sees a tyrant devouring the property of an absent Muslim and he repels him by giving up part of it, he is a benefactor (muhsin), and he is not liable for compensation for what he gave to the tyrant, for certainly he is a benefactor, and there is no way (blame) against the good-doers. Likewise, if he sees an edible animal belonging to another dying and slaughters it, he is a benefactor and is not liable for it. Similarly the wall belonging to two orphaned boys, whose father was righteous, is a matter people know, but it was hidden from Musa. Likewise the disbelief of a child may be known to people, even to his parents, but out of their love for him they do not object to him and he does not accept from them. If this is the case, then the verse is no proof that he was killed because of expected disbelief. Even if it is assumed that the boy never would have disbelieved at all, yet it was foreknown in Allah's knowledge that he would disbelieve when he reached adulthood, and Allah informed al-Khidr of this.

Someone may say: He killed him in actuality, like Nuh's killing of the children of the disbelievers through his answered supplication, which drowned the people of the earth when he knew that their fathers would only beget a wicked disbeliever; so he prayed against them with general destruction to repel the evil of their children in the future.

His saying, ﴿nor will they beget any but wicked disbelievers﴾, does not contradict their being born upon the sound fitrah, for his saying "﴿wicked, disbelieving﴾" are two circumstantial clauses destined (hal muqaddarah), meaning: those who will be wicked and disbelieve.

"If you know from them what al-Khidr knew about that boy, then kill them; otherwise, do not."

Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih.

But it may be said: The principle of the sharia and of recompense is that Allah the Glorified does not punish His servants for what He knows they will do; rather He does not punish them except after they have done what they know He forbade, and He warned them in advance of punishment for doing it. The story of al-Khidr contains nothing of knowledge of the unseen that none knows but Allah; it contains only his knowledge of causes that necessitate their rulings. Musa did not know those causes, such as al-Khidr's knowledge that the ship belonged to poor people and that behind them was a tyrannical king who would seize any sound ship; so making a hole in it was to save it entirely, then it would be restored, one of the best rulings, and it is the repelling of the greater of two evils by accepting the lesser of them. On this basis, if a person sees a tyrant devouring the property of an absent Muslim and he repels him by giving up part of it, he is a benefactor (muhsin), and he is not liable for compensation for what he gave to the tyrant, for certainly he is a benefactor, and there is no way (blame) against the good-doers. Likewise, if he sees an edible animal belonging to another dying and slaughters it, he is a benefactor and is not liable for it. Similarly the wall belonging to two orphaned boys, whose father was righteous, is a matter people know, but it was hidden from Musa. Likewise the disbelief of a child may be known to people, even to his parents, but out of their love for him they do not object to him and he does not accept from them. If this is the case, then the verse is no proof that he was killed because of expected disbelief. Even if it is assumed that the boy never would have disbelieved at all, yet it was foreknown in Allah's knowledge that he would disbelieve when he reached adulthood, and Allah informed al-Khidr of this.

Someone may say: He killed him in actuality, like Nuh's killing of the children of the disbelievers through his answered supplication, which drowned the people of the earth when he knew that their fathers would only beget a wicked disbeliever; so he prayed against them with general destruction to repel the evil of their children in the future.

His saying, ﴿nor will they beget any but wicked disbelievers﴾, does not contradict their being born upon the sound fitrah, for his saying "﴿wicked, disbelieving﴾" are two circumstantial clauses destined (hal muqaddarah), meaning: those who will be wicked and disbelieve.

This includes two meanings.

The first: their eyes are under a covering from what the Reminder (al-Dhikr) contains of the signs of God, the proofs of His oneness, and the wonders of His power.

The second: the eyes of their hearts are under a covering from understanding the Qur'an, reflecting upon it, and being guided by it.

This covering is first upon the heart, then it spreads from it to the eye.

[Section heading: The Difference Between Trust and Delusion]

The difference between trust (al-thiqah) and delusion (al-ghurrah) is this: trust is a tranquility that rests upon proofs and signs, in which the heart settles. Whenever those signs grow stronger, the trust grows stronger and more firmly established, especially with abundant experience and sound discernment. The word (ثقة, thiqah) seems, and Allah knows best, to derive from (وثاق, wathaq), meaning a bond or tie. The heart has bound itself to the one it trusts, relying upon him, having good opinion of him, and so it comes to be in the bond of his love, his dealings, reliance upon him, and dependence on him. It is bound to him with its heart, its spirit, and its body. When the heart travels to Allah and turns wholly to Him, it becomes bound by His love and enters the bond of servanthood, so it has no refuge in calamities other than Him and no shelter besides Him.

He becomes its equipment, its strength, and its treasure in its calamities, its refuge in its misfortunes, and its helper in its needs and necessities.

As for delusion (ghurrah): it is the state of the deluded person whom his soul, his Satan, his desire, and his false, vain hope regarding his Lord have deceived, until he follows his soul's desires and wishes for vain fancies from Allah. Delusion is trusting in one who is not trustworthy and resting upon one from whom hope of benefit cannot be expected, from a place that brings no good. It is like the state of one deceived by a mirage. Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

And Allah, the Exalted, says in describing the deluded:

﴿Say, "Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think that they are doing well in their work."﴾

When the veil is lifted and the realities of matters become established, these people will know that they were not upon anything: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been counting upon.﴾

There is a well-known report: "If you see Allah, glorified is He, increasing you in His blessings while you persist in disobeying Him, then beware of it, for it is merely a gradual leading (istidraj) by which He draws you on."

The evidence for this in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair.﴾ And this is among the greatest forms of delusion: that you see blessings continuing to be bestowed upon you while you persist in what displeases Him. Satan is entrusted with delusion, and the nature of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah) is to be deceived. When opinion, transgression, needy judgment, Satan's delusion, and the deluded soul come together, there is no disagreement there. The devils deluded those who are deluded about Allah, and made them hopeful while they persisted in what angers and displeases Allah, relying on His pardon and forgiveness. They spoke to them of repentance so that their hearts would be at ease, then they put them off with procrastination until the appointed time came upon them suddenly, and they were seized in their worst condition. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And false hopes deluded you until the command of Allah came, and the Deceiver deluded you about Allah.﴾

Allah, the Exalted, says: {O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life delude you, and let not the Deceiver delude you concerning Allah.} And the greatest of people in delusion regarding their Lord is one who, when Allah touches him with mercy and favor from Him, says: "This is due to my Lord"—meaning, "I am worthy of it and deserving of it, and entitled to it."

Then he said: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come.﴾ So he assumed that he deserved the blessings bestowed upon him, despite his disbelief in Allah. Then he increased in his delusion, saying: ﴿And even if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best (reward).﴾

Meaning, Paradise and honor. Thus is delusion regarding Allah. The one deluded by Satan is deluded by his promises and wishes, and his delusion by his worldly life and his soul has aided it, so he continues thus until he plunges into the pits of destruction.

(Benefit)

If a person usurps wealth and uses it to build a ribat, a mosque, or a bridge, does that benefit him, or does the reward go to the one from whom it was seized?

Ibn 'Aqil said: "There is no reward for either of them. As for the usurper, he bears the punishment, and all his dealings with another's property are repeated sins.

As for the owner of the wealth, there is no basis for his reward, because he had no intention or hisbah (seeking reward) in that building, and whatever a responsible person has neither done nor intended, he is not rewarded for it. Rather, his usurper will be held accountable on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be taken from his good deeds in proportion to his wealth."

I say: There is room to examine this, because the benefit that accrues to people arises from this person's wealth, that person's work, and the usurper's action. Although the usurper is punished for his wrongdoing and transgression, and the wronged party takes from his good deeds, what arises of benefit to people through his action and the usurped wealth is still his—for had he usurped it and spent it in sin, he would have incurred two punishments. But when he usurps it and gives it in charity, or builds a ribat or mosque with it, or ransoms a captive with it, he has done both good and evil: ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾

As for the reward of the owner of the wealth: although he did not intend that, it arises from wealth he earned, so good has come from it. Also, the seizure of his wealth is a calamity, and when it is spent in good, good has come from that calamity to him. Calamities that produce good do not deprive their owner of reward, just as deeds that produce good are rewarded even if the doer did not intend them. So calamities that produce good are not barred from being rewarded even if he did not intend them. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Deeds of Servants]
[The deeds of servants are of four kinds, of which only one is accepted]
His statement: "Indeed, Allah accepts from the servants only that which is done purely for Him."
The deeds are four: one accepted and three rejected. The accepted deed is that which is done purely for Allah and in conformity with the Sunnah (the prophetic way). The rejected deed is that which lacks one or both of these two qualities. This is because the accepted deed is that which Allah loves and is pleased with, and He, glory be to Him, loves only what He has commanded and what is done seeking His Face. Other deeds He does not love; rather, He abhors them and abhors their doers. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].
Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said: "It is the most sincere (akhlas) and the most correct (aswab) of deeds." He was asked about the meaning of this, and he said: "Indeed, if a deed is sincere but not correct, it is not accepted; and if it is correct but not sincere, it is not accepted. Until it is both sincere and correct. Sincere means that it is for Allah, and correct means that it is in accordance with the Sunnah." Then he recited His statement: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110].
If it is said: It has become clear from this that a deed done for other than Allah is rejected and not accepted, and a deed done for Allah alone is accepted. So there remains another category, namely one who does a deed both for Allah and for others, so it is neither purely for Allah nor purely for people. What is the ruling on this category? Does the whole deed become void, or does only that part which is for other than Allah become void while that which is for Allah remains valid?
It is said: This category has three types beneath it:
The first: that the initial motive for the deed is sincerity, and then showing-off (riya') and the intention of other than Allah arise during it. The ruling here rests on the initial motive, so long as one does not cancel it by a firm intention for other than Allah. Its ruling is then like that of breaking the intention during the act of worship and annulling it, I mean ceasing to maintain its ruling.
The second: the reverse of this, namely that the initial motive is for other than Allah, and then the intention is turned toward Allah. This does not count in its favour for what came before of the deed, but it is counted for him from the moment of the turning of his intention. Then, if the act of worship cannot be validly completed unless its beginning is valid, repetition is obligatory, as in the prayer. Otherwise it is not obligatory, like one who enters the state of ihram for other than Allah and then turns his intention to Allah during the standing (at 'Arafah) and the circumambulation.
The third: that one begins it intending both Allah and people, desiring to fulfil his obligation and also to receive reward and gratitude from people. This is like one who prays for a wage: if he were not paid, he would still pray, but he prays both for Allah and for the wage; or like one who performs Hajj so that the obligation falls from him and it is said "so-and-so performed Hajj," or who gives zakat in the same way. Such a deed is not accepted from him.
If the intention is a condition for the fall of the obligation, then he must repeat it, for the true sincerity which is a condition for the validity of the deed and for reward upon it has not been realised, and a ruling conditioned on a condition is absent when the condition is absent. Sincerity is the singling out of the intention for obedience to the One worshipped, and he was not commanded except with this. And when this is what is commanded, and he has not brought it, he remains under the obligation of the command. The clear Sunnah has indicated this, as in his saying ﷺ: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says on the Day of Resurrection: 'I am the most self-sufficient of partners in need of partners. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his partner.'" This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110].

[Section: The Third Degree: The Hope of the People of the Hearts]
He said: The third degree: the hope of the people of the hearts. It is the hope of meeting the Creator, which arouses longing, which hates and embitters life, and which renders one averse to creation.
This hope is the best and highest kind of hope. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 5].
This hope is the very essence and cream of faith, and toward it the eyes of the longing ones are fixed. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, consoled them by the coming of the term of His meeting, and set for them a term that calms their souls and reassures them.
Longing (ishtiyaq) is the journey of the heart in pursuit of its beloved.
The lovers differed: does it remain upon meeting the beloved, or does it cease? There are two opinions.
One group said: it ceases, because it only exists with absence, and it is the journey of the heart toward the beloved. When the journey ends and one is united with his beloved, he lays down the staff of longing from his shoulder, and longing becomes intimacy with Him and delight in His nearness.
Another group said: rather, it increases and does not cease upon meeting.
They said: because love grows through beholding the beauty of the beloved many times over what it was during absence. Its power is only veiled by the annihilation and bewilderment that come from witnessing the beloved; so when He is hidden from him, the authority of his yearning for Him appears. For this reason it has been said:
"The longing is greatest on a day when the tents draw near to the tents."
We have dealt with this question at length, together with its ramifications, in our great book on Love, and in the book "The Journey of the Two Emigrations." We shall return to it when we reach its station, if Allah the Exalted wills.
As for his statement "which embitters life": there is no doubt that the life of the longing one is embittered until he meets his beloved. Then his eye is comforted, and the embittering of his life is removed. Likewise he becomes utterly averse to creation, because his companion seeks intimacy with Allah and nearness to Him. He is the most averse of all things to creation, except for one among them who helps him attain this sought-after goal and brings him to it. Such a person is the most beloved of Allah's creatures to him. He takes no intimacy from creation other than this, and finds no rest in anything besides Him. So hold fast to seeking this companion with all your effort. If you do not succeed in finding him, then take Allah as your companion, and leave all people aside.
"Die of the disease of passion, or else venture forth, and knock at the quarter and the eyes, the watchers."
"Fear not the loneliness of the road when you go, and be a traveller under the protection of love."
"Restrain your soul for an hour from others; and if you are not answered in patience, then be patient."
"Fast today, and make tomorrow a day of breaking the fast, in which you meet the Beloved, thankful with joy."
"Wean your soul from all but Him, for every life after weaning is turning toward you."
"Reflect on the secret of the heart, and be shy before Allah on the day when the secrets are tested."
"Make the concern one, and Allah will suffice you for your many concerns; your Lord is capable."
"Await the day of the call of creation to Allah, their Lord, from the depths of the graves,"
"and listen to what you will be called by, with what qualities appear in the midst of the gatherings,"
"and marks that show upon the faces of creation, manifest before every beholder."
"O man of intellect, journeying is only resolve, then patient endurance supported by insights."
"How fine are these three: whoever attains them will reach, on the Day of Increase, above the pulpits."
"So strive for what you are told, the good tidings of this on the day the glad tidings are struck:
a sincere deed by the balance of revelation, with a secret there in the present heart."

[Section: Shirk in Worship]
As for shirk in worship, it is easier than this shirk and lighter in matter. It arises from one who believes that there is no god but Allah, and that none harms, benefits, gives or withholds except Allah, and that there is no god other than Him and no lord besides Him. But he does not single out Allah in his dealings and servitude. Rather, he acts sometimes for the sake of his own self-interest, sometimes for worldly pursuits, and sometimes to seek rank, standing and status in the eyes of people. Thus a portion of his deed and effort is for Allah, and a portion for his self, his desire and his whims, a portion for Satan, and a portion for creation. This is the condition of most people, and it is the shirk of which the Prophet ﷺ spoke, as related by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih: "Shirk in this Ummah is more hidden than the crawling of an ant." They said: "How can we be saved from it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Say: 'O Allah, I seek refuge in You from associating anything with You knowingly, and I seek Your forgiveness for what I do not know.'"

All showing-off is shirk. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, I am only a man like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110].

That is: just as He is one God with no god besides Him, so likewise worship should be for Him alone. Just as He is singled out in divinity, He must be singled out in servitude. Thus the righteous deed is that which is free of showing-off and bound by the Sunnah.

Among the supplications of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was: "O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them purely for Your Face, and do not let anyone have any share in them."

This shirk in worship nullifies the reward of the deed, and one may be punished for it if the deed was obligatory, for it places him in the position of one who did not perform it, so he is punished for abandoning the command. Allah, glory be to Him, only commanded worship of Him as pure worship, as He said: ﴿And they were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5].

Whoever is not sincere to Allah in his worship has not done what he was commanded; rather, what he brought is something other than what was commanded, so it is neither valid nor accepted from him. And Allah says: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in need of partners. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, it belongs to the one he associated, and I am free of it."

[Divisions of Shirk]
This shirk is divided into that which is forgiven and that which is not forgiven, and into the greater and the lesser. The first kind is divided into the minor and the major, and none of it is forgiven. Among it is associating others with Allah in love and reverence: that one loves a created being as he loves Allah. This is the shirk that Allah will not forgive, and it is the shirk of which He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals whom they love as they love Allah; but those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. And the companions of this shirk said to their gods, when they were gathered in Hellfire: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 97-98].

It is well known that they did not equate them with Him in creating, providing, causing death, giving life, sovereignty or power. They only equated them with Him in love, devotion, submission to them and humbling themselves before them. And this is the utmost ignorance and injustice. How can dust be equated with the Lord of lords? How can slaves be equated with the Owner of necks? How can the poor in essence, the weak in essence, the powerless in essence, the needy in essence, who has in himself nothing but non-existence, be equated with the self-sufficient in essence, the powerful in essence, whose self-sufficiency, power, sovereignty, existence, beneficence, knowledge, mercy and absolute, complete perfection are necessary attributes of His essence?

What injustice could be uglier than this? And what judgement could be more unjust? In that He equated, with His creation, the One who has no equal, as He said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; yet those who disbelieve equate [others] with their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

So the polytheist equated the One who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light with one who does not possess for himself or for others an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth. What a justice that embraces the greatest and ugliest of injustices!

[Section: The Reality of Shirk]
We say, and from Allah alone we seek the right course:
The reality of shirk is the assimilation of oneself to the Creator and the likening of the created to Him. This is the true meaning of tashbih (anthropomorphic likening), not the affirmation of the attributes of perfection by which Allah described Himself and by which His Messenger ﷺ described Him. Whoever Allah has turned upside down reverses the matter: Allah blinds his insight, overturns him by his own earning, and makes monotheism into likening, and likening into exaltation and obedience. So the polytheist is one who likens the created to the Creator in the specific attributes of divinity.

Indeed, among the attributes of divinity (al-ilahiyyah) is sole possession of harm, benefit, giving and withholding. This requires that supplication, fear, hope and reliance be directed to Him alone. Whoever attaches these to a created being has likened it to the Creator, and has made one who does not possess for himself any harm or benefit, nor death, nor life, nor resurrection, let alone for others, resemble the One to whom the whole affair belongs. The reins of all affairs are in His hands and their return is to Him. What He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. None can withhold what He gives, and none can give what He withholds. Rather, when He opens the door of His mercy to His servant, no one can hold it back, and when He withholds it from him, no one can send it to him.

Among the most abominable forms of likening is to liken this weak, poor being, who is dependent in his very essence, to the Powerful, the Self-Sufficient in His essence.

Among the attributes of divinity is absolute perfection from every aspect, in which there is no deficiency in any respect. This requires that all worship belong to Him alone: veneration, exaltation, awe, supplication, hope, turning back in repentance (inabah), repentance (tawbah), reliance (tawakkul) and seeking help (isti'anah), together with utmost humility combined with utmost love. All of this is required by reason, by the revealed law and by innate nature (fitrah) to be for Him alone, and it is impossible by reason, by the law and by innate nature for any of it to be for another. Whoever gives any part of this to another has likened that other to One who has no like, no equal and no rival. This is the most abominable and most false form of likening. Because of its extreme ugliness and because it contains the utmost wrong, Allah, glory be to Him, informed His servants that He will not forgive it, even though He has prescribed mercy upon Himself.

Among the attributes of divinity is servitude ('ubudiyyah), which stands upon two legs and has no stability without them: utmost love together with utmost humility. This is the completion of servitude, and the ranks of creatures in it vary according to their variation in these two foundations.

So whoever gives his love, his humility and his submission to other than Allah has likened that other to Him in His exclusive right. This is inconceivable for any revealed law to bring, and its ugliness is established in every innate nature and every intellect. However, the devils altered the innate natures and intellects of created beings, corrupted them for them, and led them astray from them. Whoever Allah had already destined for good remained upon the original fitrah. So He sent His messengers to them and sent down His books to them, in accordance with their innate natures and intellects, and they increased in light upon light. ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35].

Having understood this, among the attributes of divinity is prostration. Whoever prostrates to other than Him has likened the created being to Him.

Among these is reliance: whoever relies upon other than Him has likened him to Him.

Among these is repentance: whoever repents to other than Him has likened him to Him.

Among these is swearing by His name in glorification and veneration of Him. Whoever swears by other than Him has likened him to Him. This is concerning the aspect of likening (tashbih).

As for the aspect of imitating Him (tashabbuh bihi): whoever magnifies himself, becomes arrogant, and calls people to praise him excessively in eulogy, veneration, submission and hope, and to attach their hearts to him in fear, hope, seeking refuge and seeking help, has imitated Allah and contended with Him in His lordship and His divinity. He deserves to be humiliated to the utmost degree of humiliation, to be abased to the utmost degree of abasement, and to be placed beneath the feet of His creatures.

In the Sahih, from him (ﷺ) it is related that he said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Greatness is My waist-wrapper and majesty is My cloak. Whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will punish him.'"

If the one who makes a picture with his own hand is among the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection because of his imitation of Allah merely in the form, then what is the assumption regarding imitating Allah in lordship and divinity?

As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are the picture-makers. It will be said to them: 'Bring to life what you have created.'"

In the two Sahihs, from him (ﷺ), he said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Who is more unjust than one who sets out to create a creation like My creation? Let them create an atom, or let them create a grain of barley.'" By the atom and the grain of barley he drew attention to what is greater and more significant than them.

The point is that this is the state of one who imitates Him in making a picture; so what is the state of one who imitates Him in the exclusive attributes of His lordship and divinity? Likewise, one who imitates Him in a name that is fitting only for Allah alone, such as "King of Kings," "Judge of Judges," and the like.

It has been established in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Verily the most despised of names in the sight of Allah is a man who is called Shahan Shah," meaning "King of Kings" (malik al-muluk), "there is no king but Allah." In another wording: "The man most hateful to Allah is a man called Malik al-Amlak (King of Kings)."

This is the hatred and anger of Allah against whoever imitates Him in a name that is fitting only for Him. He, glory be to Him, is alone the King of Kings, and He alone is the Judge of Judges. He is the One who judges over all judges and decides over all of them, and there is no other.
